title: Space
blurb: Planets, stars, galaxies and the search for life.

lessons.title: The Solar System
lessons.summary: A tour of our neighbourhood, from the Sun to the edge.

cards.title: Our star
cards.text: The Sun holds about 99.8% of all the mass in the Solar System. It's a ball of hot plasma, fusing hydrogen into helium in its core at about 15 million °C.

deep.x: The Sun is an ordinary star: a medium-sized yellow dwarf, one of perhaps 100–400 billion in the Milky Way. What makes it special is simply that it's ours. It is 1.39 million km wide, about 109 times Earth's diameter, and you could fit roughly 1.3 million Earths inside it.

In the core, the temperature is about 15 million °C and the pressure is about 250 billion times the air pressure at sea level. Under those conditions, hydrogen nuclei collide hard enough to fuse into helium. Every second the Sun turns about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium, and around 4 million tonnes of mass disappear as pure energy (E = mc²).
Why it doesn't explode or collapse

The Sun is a balancing act. Gravity squeezes inwards; the heat from fusion pushes outwards. If fusion speeds up, the core expands, cools slightly and fusion slows again. This self-regulation has kept the Sun stable for about 4.6 billion years.
What it's made of

x: About 73% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass
The remaining 2% is "metals" to astronomers: oxygen, carbon, iron and more
It rotates faster at its equator (about 25 days) than at its poles (about 35 days), because it isn't solid

deep.x: The light reaching you now left the Sun's surface about 8 minutes ago, but the energy behind it took tens of thousands of years to work its way out from the core.
The Sun loses about 4 million tonnes of mass every second, yet it's so big that over its whole life it will lose less than 0.1% of its mass this way.

cards.title: Eight planets
cards.text: Four small rocky planets sit close to the Sun; four giants lie further out. A memory trick: "My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming".

deep.x: The planets formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a flat, spinning disc of gas and dust around the young Sun. Close to the Sun it was too hot for ice, so only rock and metal could clump together: that's why the inner planets are small and rocky. Beyond the "snow line", between Mars and Jupiter, ice was plentiful, so cores grew big enough to grab huge amounts of gas.

steps: Spinning disc of gas and dust

deep.x: Why they all orbit the same way
All eight planets orbit in the same direction and roughly in the same plane, because they formed from the same spinning disc. It's a fossil of the Solar System's birth.

items: Most also spin the same way

deep.x: Quick profiles

x: **Mercury**: smallest, no real atmosphere, days scorching and nights freezing
**Venus**: Earth-sized, buried under thick clouds of sulphuric acid
**Earth**: the only place known to have life and liquid surface oceans
**Mars**: cold desert with the tallest volcano and a deep canyon system
**Jupiter**: largest, a gas giant with a storm bigger than Earth
**Saturn**: famous rings, lighter than water on average
**Uranus**: tilted on its side, an icy blue-green giant
**Neptune**: farthest, darkest and windiest

deep.w: The planets line up in a neat row
deep.r: They're spread around their orbits; true alignments are rare and loose

deep.x: The mnemonic "My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming" gives the order from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

cards.title: Rocky vs giant
cards.text: The inner planets are made of rock and metal. The outer ones are gas giants (Jupiter, Saturn) and ice giants (Uranus, Neptune), with no solid surface to stand on.

deep.x: The Solar System splits neatly in two. The four inner planets are dense balls of rock around iron cores. The four outer planets are giants: mostly gas and fluids, with no surface you could stand on.
Gas giants vs ice giants

Jupiter and Saturn are mostly hydrogen and helium, like the Sun. Uranus and Neptune contain much more water, ammonia and methane, compressed into hot, dense fluids. Astronomers call those "ices" even though they aren't frozen.
What's inside Jupiter

Going down into Jupiter, the gas gets denser and hotter until hydrogen is squeezed into a liquid metal that conducts electricity. Swirling metallic hydrogen generates Jupiter's magnetic field, the strongest of any planet.
Why the split?

x: Near the Sun, only rock and metal could stay solid
Farther out, ice added extra building material, so cores grew faster
Big cores (about 10 Earth masses) could pull in surrounding gas before the young Sun blew it away

deep.x: Jupiter's magnetic field is about 20,000 times stronger than Earth's, and its radiation belts would be lethal to an unshielded astronaut.

cards.title: Venus is the hottest
cards.text: Venus is further from the Sun than Mercury but hotter, about 465 °C, because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect.

deep.x: Venus shows what a runaway greenhouse effect can do. Its atmosphere is about 96% carbon dioxide and so thick that the surface pressure is 92 times Earth's, like being 900 metres under the sea.
How the trap works

Sunlight that gets through the clouds warms the ground. The ground gives off infrared heat, but CO₂ absorbs it and sends much of it back down. With so much CO₂, almost no heat escapes, and the whole planet sits at around 465 °C, day and night, poles and equator.

steps: Surface hot enough to melt lead

deep.x: Earth's twin gone wrong

Venus is almost Earth's size and was probably once much more like it, possibly with oceans. Being closer to the Sun, its water evaporated, strengthening the greenhouse effect until the oceans boiled away and the hydrogen leaked into space.
Other oddities

x: Venus spins backwards compared with most planets, so the Sun rises in the west
A day on Venus (243 Earth days) is longer than its year (225 Earth days)
Clouds of sulphuric acid race around the planet in about four days
Soviet Venera landers survived on the surface for only up to about two hours

deep.w: Mercury must be hottest because it's closest to the Sun
deep.r: Venus is hotter, thanks to its thick CO₂ atmosphere

deep.x: Distance from the Sun isn't everything: an atmosphere can matter more.

cards.title: Jupiter, the giant
cards.text: Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined. Its Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than Earth that has lasted for centuries.

deep.x: Jupiter has 318 times Earth's mass, more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined. If it had been about 80 times more massive, it could have become a small star.
The Great Red Spot

The Great Red Spot is a giant anticyclone, a high-pressure storm, wider than Earth. It has been observed since at least the 1830s, maybe since 1665, but it's shrinking: it was about three Earths wide in the 1800s.
A fast spinner
Despite its size, Jupiter spins once in under 10 hours, the fastest of any planet. The spin flattens it visibly at the poles and stretches its clouds into the striped bands we see.
Moons and missions

x: About 95 known moons, including the four large Galilean moons Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto
Galileo discovered those four in 1610, proving not everything orbits Earth
NASA's Juno has orbited Jupiter since 2016, mapping its interior and poles
ESA's JUICE, launched 2023, will study the icy moons in the 2030s

deep.x: Jupiter doesn't strictly orbit the Sun's centre: the Sun and Jupiter both orbit a shared balance point just outside the Sun's surface.

cards.title: Saturn's rings
cards.text: Saturn's rings are made of countless chunks of ice and rock, from dust to house-sized. They're about 280,000 km wide but in places only about 10 metres thick.

deep.x: Saturn's rings are mostly water ice, from tiny grains to chunks the size of a house. They stretch about 280,000 km across, almost three-quarters of the distance from Earth to the Moon, yet are often only about 10 metres thick. If the rings were a sheet of paper, they'd be far thinner than paper relative to their width.
How old are they?

Data from the Cassini spacecraft suggested the rings could be young, perhaps only a few hundred million years old, because they look clean and bright. Other scientists argue rings can stay clean for billions of years. It's still debated.
Where rings come from
Rings likely formed when a moon or comet came too close and was torn apart by Saturn's gravity. Inside a zone called the Roche limit, tidal forces stop material clumping into a moon.
Rings everywhere

x: All four giant planets have rings; Saturn's are simply the brightest
Gaps are cleared by small "shepherd moons" orbiting within the rings
The rings are slowly raining onto Saturn and may vanish in a few hundred million years

deep.x: Every 13–15 years Earth passes through the plane of Saturn's rings, and they almost disappear from view because they're so thin.

cards.title: Pluto, demoted
cards.text: In 2006 the International Astronomical Union defined a planet as a body that has cleared its orbit. Pluto shares its zone with many icy objects, so it became a dwarf planet.

deep.x: For 76 years Pluto was the ninth planet. Then astronomers began finding similar icy worlds beyond Neptune, in the Kuiper Belt. In 2005 they found Eris, about the same size as Pluto. Either it was a tenth planet, or the definition had to change.
The three rules
In 2006 the International Astronomical Union said a planet must meet three criteria. Pluto passes the first two but fails the third.

items: Round, shaped by its own gravity

deep.x: What New Horizons found

In 2015 NASA's New Horizons flew past Pluto and revealed a surprisingly active world: a heart-shaped plain of nitrogen ice, mountains of water ice, a thin hazy atmosphere and signs of a possible underground ocean.
Still controversial

x: Some planetary scientists prefer a geology-based definition: any round world is a planet
Under that rule, the Solar System would have dozens of planets
Officially, there are five recognised dwarf planets: Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake

deep.w: Pluto was demoted because it's too small
deep.r: It hasn't cleared its orbit of other objects

deep.x: Science reclassifies things when new evidence shows the old categories no longer fit.

cards.title: Asteroids and comets
cards.text: Asteroids are rocky leftovers, mostly between Mars and Jupiter. Comets are icy bodies from the outer Solar System that grow glowing tails when they near the Sun.

deep.x: Asteroids and comets are leftovers from the formation of the planets, 4.6 billion years old. Studying them is like reading the Solar System's original building materials.
Asteroid types

x: **C-type**: dark, carbon-rich, the most common
**S-type**: stony, made of silicate minerals
**M-type**: metallic, possibly cores of shattered protoplanets

deep.x: A comet's journey

Most of the time a comet is a dark, frozen lump far from the Sun. As it approaches, sunlight turns ice directly into gas, which drags dust out with it. That creates a glowing coma and two tails: a straight blue ion tail pushed by the solar wind, and a curved, yellowish dust tail.
Samples brought home

Missions have collected pieces of asteroids and returned them to Earth: Japan's Hayabusa2 from Ryugu (2020) and NASA's OSIRIS-REx from Bennu (2023). Bennu's sample contained water-bearing minerals and organic molecules, ingredients for life.
Comets and water-rich asteroids may have delivered some of Earth's water and organic molecules early in its history.

cards.title: Distances
cards.text: Astronomers measure the Solar System in astronomical units: 1 AU is the Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million km. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us.

deep.x: Space distances are so large that kilometres become clumsy. Astronomers use the astronomical unit (AU), the average Earth–Sun distance of about 149.6 million km, for the Solar System, and light-years for the stars.
Light travel times

x: Moon: 1.3 seconds
Sun: 8 minutes 20 seconds
Jupiter: 35–52 minutes, depending on positions
Neptune: about 4 hours
Voyager 1: over 23 hours

v.unit: light travel time from the Sun, minutes

deep.x: How we measure it

Astronomers bounce radar off Venus and asteroids and time the echo, giving the AU to within metres. For nearby stars, they use parallax: the tiny shift in a star's position as Earth moves around the Sun.
Communicating with distant spacecraft is slow: commands to a Mars rover can take up to 24 minutes to arrive, so rovers must drive partly by themselves.
Travelling at motorway speed, 120 km/h, it would take about 140 years to drive to the Sun.

cards.title: A model in a football stadium
cards.text: Shrink the Sun to a football in the centre circle. Earth is a peppercorn about 25 m away, Jupiter a marble about 130 m away, and Neptune a small bead about 715 m away.

deep.x: Scale models reveal just how empty the Solar System is. Shrink the Sun to a football 22 cm wide, about 6.3 billion times smaller than reality, and every distance shrinks by the same factor.

x: Scale = 1 : 6.3 billion
Earth–Sun 150 million km → 24 m
Earth 12,742 km → 2 mm

deep.x: Where everything goes

x: **Mercury**: a grain of sand, 9 m away
**Venus** and **Earth**: two peppercorns, 17 m and 24 m away
**Mars**: a pinhead, 36 m away
**Jupiter**: a marble, 124 m away
**Saturn**: a smaller marble, 227 m away
**Uranus** and **Neptune**: two peas or beads, 455 m and 715 m away

deep.x: And the nearest star?
On the same scale, Proxima Centauri would be another football about 6,400 km away, farther than from Lisbon to New York.

deep.w: Space is crowded like in films
deep.r: The Solar System is almost entirely empty space

deep.x: Try it: pace out the distances in a park with a ball and some peppercorns. It's the best way to feel the scale.

quiz.explain: Its thick CO₂ atmosphere traps heat.

quiz.q: How long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
quiz.explain: The Sun is 150 million km away.

lessons.title: Stars and galaxies
lessons.summary: How stars live and die, and where we are in the universe.

cards.title: A star is born
cards.text: Stars form inside giant clouds of gas and dust. Gravity pulls a clump together until the core is hot and dense enough to fuse hydrogen, and a star lights up.

deep.x: Stars are born inside giant molecular clouds: cold (around −260 °C), dark clouds of hydrogen and dust that can be hundreds of light-years across. They sit quietly until something disturbs them, such as the shock wave of a nearby supernova or a collision between clouds.
From clump to star

As a clump collapses, it spins faster, like a skater pulling in their arms, and flattens into a disc. The centre heats up into a protostar that glows from the energy of collapse, not yet from fusion. For a Sun-like star this stage lasts tens of millions of years.
Stellar nurseries

x: The Orion Nebula, 1,300 light-years away, is the nearest big star-forming region, visible with binoculars
Webb's infrared images show "pillars" of dust with newborn stars hidden inside
Stars form in clusters; the Sun's birth siblings have since drifted apart

deep.x: The leftover disc around a newborn star is where planets form, so star birth and planet birth are one process.
The Milky Way makes only a few new stars a year on average, a few Suns' worth of mass, but over billions of years that adds up to hundreds of billions.

cards.title: Fusion
cards.text: Stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium. A little mass is turned into a lot of energy, following Einstein's E = mc².

deep.x: In a star's core, hydrogen nuclei (protons) are moving so fast that they overcome their electric repulsion and stick together. Through a chain of steps, four protons end up as one helium nucleus. The helium weighs about 0.7% less than the four protons that made it; that missing mass becomes energy.

steps: 0.7% of the mass released as energy

deep.x: Why it takes a star

On Earth, protons repel each other far too strongly. Only the crushing gravity of a whole star creates the temperature (~15 million °C) and density needed. Even then, quantum "tunnelling" is required: protons sneak through the repulsion barrier by chance.
Heavier fuels

x: Bigger stars also fuse helium into carbon and oxygen, then heavier elements
Each stage burns faster: a massive star may fuse silicon into iron in about a day
Iron is the end of the line: fusing it consumes energy instead of releasing it

deep.w: The Sun is burning like a fire
deep.r: It's nuclear fusion, not chemical burning; there's no oxygen fire

deep.x: Fusion is why the Sun can shine for 10 billion years: a chemical fire the size of the Sun would burn out in a few thousand.

cards.title: Star colours
cards.text: A star's colour shows its temperature: red stars are the coolest, blue the hottest. Our Sun is a yellowish-white star in the middle.

deep.x: Heat anything enough and it glows: first red, then orange, yellow, white and finally blue-white. A blacksmith judges iron's temperature by colour; astronomers judge stars the same way. The peak colour of a star's light tells us its surface temperature.
Spectral classes
Astronomers sort stars into classes O, B, A, F, G, K and M, from hottest to coolest. The Sun is a G2 star. Students remember the order with "Oh Be A Fine Girl/Guy, Kiss Me".

items.b: orange and red, cool, most common

deep.x: Colour, size and life

x: Blue stars are massive and burn fuel fast: they live only millions of years
Red dwarfs are small and frugal: they can shine for trillions of years
About three-quarters of all stars are red dwarfs, too faint to see with the naked eye

deep.w: The Sun is yellow
deep.r: Seen from space it's white; our atmosphere makes it look yellow

deep.x: Hot, heavy stars live fast and die young; cool, small stars live almost forever.

cards.title: Life of a star like the Sun
cards.text: The Sun is about halfway through a 10-billion-year life. In about 5 billion years it will swell into a red giant, then shed its outer layers and leave a small white dwarf.

deep.x: A star spends most of its life on the "main sequence", steadily fusing hydrogen in its core. The Sun is about 4.6 billion years into a roughly 10-billion-year main-sequence life, and it's slowly getting brighter, about 10% every billion years.
The red giant phase

When the core runs out of hydrogen, it contracts and heats up while the outer layers swell enormously. The Sun will grow about 200 times wider, swallowing Mercury and Venus and possibly Earth. It will then fuse helium into carbon in its core.
The gentle ending

Eventually the outer layers drift away as a glowing shell called a planetary nebula, lit by the exposed core. That core, a white dwarf about Earth's size but with half the Sun's mass, slowly cools for billions of years.

x: A teaspoon of white-dwarf material would weigh several tonnes on Earth
"Planetary nebula" is a misleading old name: they have nothing to do with planets

deep.x: Earth will become uninhabitable long before the red giant stage, as the slowly brightening Sun boils away the oceans in about a billion years.

cards.title: Death of a giant star
cards.text: Stars much heavier than the Sun end in a supernova explosion that can briefly outshine a galaxy. The core becomes a neutron star or, if heavy enough, a black hole.

deep.x: Stars more than about 8 times the Sun's mass end violently. They fuse heavier and heavier elements in layers like an onion, until the core is iron. Iron fusion produces no energy, so the core suddenly loses its support.
Collapse and explosion

The iron core, about the mass of the Sun but the size of Earth, collapses in under a second to a ball about 20 km wide. Infalling layers bounce off this ultra-dense core and, driven by a flood of neutrinos, the star blows itself apart in a supernova.
What's left

x: **Neutron star**: a city-sized ball of neutrons; a teaspoon would weigh about a billion tonnes
**Pulsar**: a spinning neutron star sweeping beams of radio waves, like a lighthouse
**Black hole**: if the remaining core is heavy enough, nothing stops the collapse

deep.x: In 1054 Chinese astronomers recorded a "guest star" visible in daylight for weeks. Its remains are the Crab Nebula, with a pulsar spinning 30 times a second at its heart.
Betelgeuse, Orion's red shoulder, will explode as a supernova sometime in the next 100,000 years, bright enough to cast shadows at night.

cards.title: We are stardust
cards.text: Most of the atoms in your body, like carbon, oxygen and iron, were made inside stars that exploded before the Sun was born.

deep.x: The Big Bang made almost only hydrogen and helium, plus a trace of lithium. Every heavier atom, the carbon in your DNA, the oxygen you breathe, the calcium in your bones, the iron in your blood, was forged later inside stars and scattered into space when they died.

items: Massive stars and supernovae: oxygen to iron

deep.x: The cosmic recycling loop
Dying stars blow enriched gas into space. That gas mixes into new clouds, which form new stars and planets with more heavy elements than before. The Sun is at least a third-generation star.
Gold from collisions

In 2017, detectors caught gravitational waves from two neutron stars colliding 130 million light-years away. Telescopes then saw the explosion's light, full of freshly made heavy elements such as gold and platinum.

x: The hydrogen in your body is about 13.8 billion years old
About 99% of your body's atoms by count are hydrogen, oxygen, carbon or nitrogen
Every heavier element in your body passed through at least one star

deep.x: Carl Sagan put it simply: "We are made of star-stuff."

cards.title: Black holes
cards.text: A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope took the first image of one, in the galaxy M87.

deep.x: A black hole forms when a lot of mass is squeezed into a small space, so that the escape velocity, the speed needed to get away, exceeds the speed of light. Since nothing can travel faster than light, nothing escapes from inside the boundary called the event horizon.
Not cosmic vacuum cleaners

From a distance, a black hole's gravity is no stronger than any object of the same mass. If the Sun were replaced by a black hole of the same mass, Earth would keep orbiting exactly as now, just in darkness.

deep.w: Black holes suck everything in
deep.r: Far away, their gravity is like any object of the same mass

deep.x: The 2019 image

The Event Horizon Telescope linked radio dishes across the planet into an Earth-sized telescope. It imaged the glowing ring of hot gas around M87*, a black hole 6.5 billion times the Sun's mass, 55 million light-years away. The dark centre is the black hole's "shadow".
Types of black holes

x: **Stellar**: a few to tens of Suns, left by dying massive stars
**Supermassive**: millions to billions of Suns, at the centres of galaxies
**Intermediate**: hundreds to thousands of Suns, rarer and harder to find

deep.x: Inside the event horizon, the direction "towards the centre" becomes like the direction "towards the future": unavoidable.

cards.title: Light-years
cards.text: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year: about 9.5 trillion km. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.

deep.x: A light-year is a distance, not a time: how far light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion km. Light moves at 299,792 km per second, fast enough to circle Earth seven and a half times in a second.

x: 299,792 km/s × 31.6 million s
≈ 9.46 trillion km
= 1 light-year

deep.x: Distances in the galaxy
Other units
Professional astronomers often use the parsec: about 3.26 light-years. It comes from parallax, the distance at which a star shifts by one arcsecond as Earth moves around the Sun.
Looking back in time
Because light takes time to arrive, looking far away means looking into the past. We see Proxima Centauri as it was 4.2 years ago and the most distant galaxies as they were over 13 billion years ago.

deep.w: A light-year is a unit of time
deep.r: It measures distance

deep.x: The fastest spacecraft ever, Parker Solar Probe, would still take over 6,000 years to cover the 4.2 light-years to Proxima Centauri.

cards.title: The Milky Way
cards.text: Our galaxy is a barred spiral of 100–400 billion stars, about 100,000 light-years across. The Sun sits in a quiet arm about 26,000 light-years from the centre.

deep.x: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy: a central bar of old stars, a bulge, a thin disc with spiral arms full of gas and young stars, and a faint halo of old stars and globular clusters. Surrounding it all is an invisible halo of dark matter that outweighs the stars many times over.
Our address

The Sun lies in the Orion Spur, a minor arm between the Sagittarius and Perseus arms, about 26,000 light-years from the centre. It orbits the centre at about 230 km/s, once every ~230 million years. The last time the Sun was here, the first dinosaurs were appearing.
The centre

At the very centre lies Sagittarius A*, a black hole of about 4 million Suns. Astronomers proved it by tracking stars orbiting an invisible object at thousands of km/s, work that won the 2020 Nobel Prize.

x: Thick dust blocks our visible view of the centre; infrared and radio see through
Gaia, an ESA spacecraft, has mapped over 1.8 billion stars in 3D

deep.x: Within the next few billion years the Milky Way may merge with the Andromeda galaxy. Stars are so far apart that direct star collisions will be extremely rare.

cards.title: Billions of galaxies
cards.text: The observable universe holds perhaps 100 billion to 2 trillion galaxies. The Andromeda galaxy, 2.5 million light-years away, is the furthest thing you can see with the naked eye.

deep.x: In 1995 the Hubble Space Telescope stared at a tiny, apparently empty patch of sky for ten days. The Hubble Deep Field revealed about 3,000 galaxies in a speck the size of a tennis ball seen from 100 metres away. Scaled to the whole sky, the observable universe holds hundreds of billions of galaxies, perhaps up to 2 trillion including faint dwarfs.
Galaxy shapes
Groups and clusters

Galaxies gather in groups and clusters. The Milky Way belongs to the Local Group of about 80 galaxies, dominated by Andromeda and us. The Local Group is part of the Virgo Supercluster and the larger Laniakea supercluster.

x: Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away and contains around a trillion stars
It's approaching us at about 110 km/s
On a dark night it's a faint smudge, the most distant object easily seen by eye

deep.x: Every star you see with the naked eye is in our own galaxy; Andromeda is the one galaxy beyond it you can easily spot.

quiz.q: What powers stars?
Which colour stars are the hottest?
What will the Sun become at the end of its life?
quiz.explain: It's not massive enough to explode.

lessons.title: Space exploration
lessons.summary: From Sputnik to Mars rovers.

cards.title: The Space Race
cards.text: After the Second World War, the USA and the Soviet Union competed to reach space first. The Soviets launched the first satellite and the first human; the Americans landed on the Moon.

deep.x: The Space Race grew out of Cold War rivalry. Rockets built to carry nuclear warheads could also carry satellites and people, and each superpower wanted to prove its system was superior. Sputnik 1, a 58 cm metal ball beeping radio signals, shocked the West in October 1957.
Soviet firsts

x: First satellite (Sputnik 1, 1957) and first animal in orbit (Laika, 1957)
First human in space (Yuri Gagarin, 1961) and first woman (Valentina Tereshkova, 1963)
First spacewalk (Alexei Leonov, 1965) and first landing on another planet (Venera 7, Venus, 1970)

deep.x: The American response

The USA created NASA in 1958 and, in 1961, President Kennedy set the goal of landing a man on the Moon before the decade was out. At its peak, Apollo employed about 400,000 people and took over 4% of the US federal budget.

v.unit: % of US federal budget for NASA (approx.)

deep.x: From rivals to partners
The race ended in cooperation: the Apollo–Soyuz handshake in orbit in 1975, then the International Space Station, built by the USA, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada.
Competition drove astonishing speed: only 12 years separated Sputnik from footprints on the Moon.

cards.title: How rockets work

steps: Hot gas rushes out the back

cards.text: Rockets push hot gas out of the back at high speed; by Newton's third law, the gas pushes the rocket forward. They work in a vacuum because they carry their own oxygen.

deep.x: A rocket is a controlled explosion pointed in one direction. Fuel and an oxidiser burn in a chamber; the hot gas expands and rushes out through a bell-shaped nozzle at several kilometres per second. Pushing gas backwards pushes the rocket forwards: Newton's third law.

deep.w: Rockets push against the air
deep.r: They push against their own exhaust, so they work best in a vacuum

deep.x: Fuel choices

items.b: simple boosters, can't be switched off

deep.x: The tyranny of the rocket equation

Most of a rocket is fuel: to reach orbit, roughly 85–90% of the launch mass is propellant. Carrying more fuel means carrying fuel to lift that fuel. That's why rockets drop empty stages on the way up.
Staging

x: The first stage lifts the heavy rocket through the thick lower atmosphere
It drops away when empty, and the lighter upper stage continues
Each stage sheds dead weight so the rest can go faster

deep.x: The Saturn V that launched Apollo 11 was 111 m tall and weighed about 2,900 tonnes at launch, nearly all of it propellant.

cards.title: Getting to orbit
cards.text: To orbit, you need to go sideways fast enough to keep "falling" around the Earth without hitting it: about 7.8 km/s, or 28,000 km/h, in low orbit.

deep.x: Imagine Newton's cannon on a very tall mountain. Fire slowly and the ball lands nearby. Fire faster and it lands farther away. At about 7.8 km/s, the ground curves away as fast as the ball falls: it never lands. That's an orbit.
Up is easy, sideways is hard

Reaching 100 km, the edge of space, takes a few minutes and modest energy; suborbital tourist flights do it. Staying there requires going sideways at 28,000 km/h, which needs about 30 times more energy. That's why rockets tilt over soon after launch.
Helpful tricks

x: Launching eastward borrows Earth's spin, up to 465 m/s at the equator
That's why launch sites are often near the equator, like Kourou in French Guiana
Launching over the sea keeps falling stages away from people

v.unit: free speed from Earth's spin, m/s

deep.x: Getting to low orbit is "halfway to anywhere": most of the energy of a deep-space trip is spent just reaching orbit.

cards.title: Apollo 11
cards.text: On 20 July 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon while Michael Collins orbited above. Twelve people walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972.

deep.x: Apollo 11 launched from Florida on 16 July 1969 on a Saturn V. After three days it entered lunar orbit. Armstrong and Aldrin descended in the lunar module *Eagle* while Collins stayed in the command module *Columbia*.
A tense landing

During descent, the guidance computer flashed "1202" and "1201" alarms: it was overloaded. Mission Control judged it safe to continue. Armstrong then flew manually past a boulder field and landed with about 25 seconds of fuel left before an abort decision.
What they did

x: Planted a flag and a plaque: "We came in peace for all mankind"
Set up a seismometer and a laser reflector still used to measure the Moon's distance
Collected rock and soil samples showing the Moon is about 4.5 billion years old

deep.x: Six landings in all

deep.w: The Moon landings were faked
deep.r: Rocks, retroreflectors and independent tracking, including by the USSR, confirm them

deep.x: The Apollo guidance computer had about 4 KB of RAM. A modern phone is millions of times more powerful.

cards.title: The International Space Station
cards.text: The ISS has been continuously crewed since November 2000. It's about the size of a football pitch and circles the Earth about 16 times a day.

deep.x: The ISS is the largest structure humans have built in space: about 109 m across and around 420 tonnes. It was assembled from 1998 in more than 40 missions by the USA, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada, and has been continuously occupied since 2 November 2000.
Life aboard

Crews of about seven live and work for around six months. Each day they see 16 sunrises and sunsets as they orbit at about 28,000 km/h, 400 km up. The station needs regular engine burns to stay up, because thin air at that height slowly drags it down.
What it's for

x: Medical research on how bodies cope with weightlessness, for future Mars trips
Experiments in materials, fluids and plants that behave differently without gravity
Testing life-support and recycling systems
A place for international cooperation

deep.x: What comes next
The ISS is due to be de-orbited around 2030, guided into a remote part of the Pacific. Commercial stations are planned to replace it, and China operates its own station, Tiangong.
You can see the ISS with the naked eye: it looks like a bright, steady star crossing the sky in a few minutes. Apps tell you when it passes overhead.

cards.title: Space telescopes
cards.text: Above the atmosphere, telescopes see more clearly. Hubble (1990) transformed astronomy; James Webb (2021) sees infrared light from the first galaxies.

deep.x: Earth's atmosphere blurs starlight (that's why stars twinkle) and blocks most ultraviolet, X-rays and much of the infrared. Telescopes in space escape both problems.
Hubble's rescue

Hubble's mirror was ground slightly wrong: off by about 1/50th of a hair's width, enough to blur its images. In 1993 astronauts fitted corrective optics, like glasses. Five servicing missions kept it working for over three decades.
Webb's tricks

x: Its mirror, made of 18 gold-coated segments, folded up to fit in the rocket
A five-layer sunshield the size of a tennis court keeps it below −220 °C
Cold matters because warm objects glow in infrared, which would swamp faint signals

deep.x: What they've shown us

Hubble pinned down the age of the universe and showed that its expansion is accelerating. Webb sees galaxies from just a few hundred million years after the Big Bang and analyses the air of exoplanets.
Webb can detect the heat of a bumblebee at the distance of the Moon.

cards.title: Robots on Mars
cards.text: Rovers have explored Mars since 1997. Perseverance, landed in 2021, collects rock samples and carried Ingenuity, the first helicopter to fly on another planet.

deep.x: Rovers are the only way to explore Mars' surface so far. Each generation has been bigger and smarter: from the microwave-sized Sojourner to car-sized Curiosity and Perseverance, powered by nuclear batteries.
Opportunity, the marathon rover
Opportunity was designed for 90 Martian days. It lasted almost 15 years and drove over 45 km, a marathon, before a dust storm cut its solar power in 2018.
Searching for past life

Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater, an ancient lake with a river delta, the kind of place where microbes might have lived. It drills rock cores and seals them in tubes for a future mission to bring back to Earth.
Ingenuity

x: A 1.8 kg helicopter that flew 72 times between 2021 and 2024, far beyond its planned 5 flights
It had to spin its blades at about 2,500 rpm, because Mars' air is only 1% as dense as Earth's
It proved powered flight is possible on another planet

deep.x: Curiosity's landing used a "sky crane": a rocket platform hovered and lowered the rover on cables, then flew away to crash safely.

cards.title: Reusable rockets
cards.text: Since 2015, rockets have landed their boosters back on Earth to fly again. Reuse has cut the cost of reaching orbit and made launches routine.

deep.x: For decades, nearly every rocket was thrown away after one flight, like flying a jet once and scrapping it. Since SpaceX first landed a Falcon 9 booster in December 2015, reusable first stages have become routine; some boosters have flown more than 25 times.
How a booster lands
Why it matters

The first stage is the most expensive part of a rocket. Reusing it, plus refurbishing quickly, has cut launch costs and multiplied launch rates. Cheaper access to space made large satellite constellations practical.

items: build a new rocket each time

x: The space shuttle was partly reusable, but needed months of costly refurbishment between flights
New rockets from several companies and countries are being designed for reuse

deep.x: Landing a booster has been compared to balancing a broomstick on your hand in a strong wind, from 70 km up.

cards.title: Voyager
cards.text: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object, more than 24 billion km away. It carries a golden record of sounds and images from Earth.

deep.x: Voyager 1 and 2 launched in 1977, using a rare planetary alignment that happens about every 176 years to swing from planet to planet. Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus and Neptune.
Still talking

Both probes are still sending data from interstellar space, beyond the Sun's protective bubble. Their signals take nearly a day to arrive and are fainter than a billionth of a billionth of a watt. They run on decaying plutonium batteries and are slowly shutting down instruments.
The golden record

Each Voyager carries a gold-plated copper record with greetings in 55 languages, music from Bach to Chuck Berry, natural sounds and 115 images, plus instructions for playing it. It's a message in a bottle for any civilisation that might find it.

x: The cover shows the record's playback speed and Earth's location relative to 14 pulsars
Carl Sagan led the committee that chose its contents

deep.x: In about 40,000 years Voyager 1 will pass within 1.6 light-years of a star called Gliese 445.

cards.title: Satellites in daily life
cards.text: Thousands of satellites support daily life: GPS navigation, weather forecasts, TV, internet and monitoring of fires and crops.

deep.x: Every day you probably use a dozen satellites without noticing. They time-stamp bank transactions, route flights, forecast rain, broadcast TV, connect ships to the internet and help farmers decide when to water.
Navigation and time
Navigation satellites carry atomic clocks. Beyond giving your position, their time signals synchronise phone networks, power grids and financial markets around the world.
Watching the planet

x: Weather satellites track storms and feed forecast models
Copernicus Sentinel satellites map floods, fires, crops and sea ice for free
Satellites measure sea-level rise to a few millimetres

deep.x: Crowded orbits
The number of active satellites has grown from about 1,000 in 2010 to well over 10,000, mostly internet constellations. That brings benefits but also risks of collisions and debris.
Without satellite timing, many ATMs, mobile networks and stock exchanges would quickly drift out of sync.

lessons.title: Earth, Moon and sky
lessons.summary: Seasons, phases, eclipses and tides.

cards.title: Why we have seasons

items.w: Closer to the Sun in summer
items.r: Earth's tilt changes the angle of sunlight

cards.text: Seasons aren't caused by distance from the Sun. Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, so each hemisphere takes turns leaning towards the Sun and getting more direct light.

deep.x: Earth's axis is tilted 23.4° relative to its orbit, and it stays pointing the same way in space (towards Polaris) all year. So for half the orbit the Northern Hemisphere leans towards the Sun, and for the other half it leans away.
Two effects of the tilt

x: **Angle**: high Sun concentrates energy on a small area; low Sun spreads the same energy thin
**Day length**: in Lisbon, the longest day has about 15 hours of daylight; the shortest about 9.5

deep.x: The distance myth
Earth's orbit is slightly elliptical, but we're actually closest to the Sun in early January, during northern winter. The difference in distance is only about 3%, too small to drive seasons.

deep.w: Summer happens when Earth is closest to the Sun
deep.r: We're closest in January; the tilt causes seasons

deep.x: Opposite hemispheres

Because the hemispheres take turns, Christmas is in summer in Brazil and Australia. At the equator, seasons are weak; near the poles, they're extreme, with midnight Sun in summer and polar night in winter.
If Earth had no tilt, there would be no seasons at all, just permanent climate bands from equator to poles.

cards.title: Day and night
cards.text: Earth spins on its axis once about every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day; the other side has night. The Sun "rises" because we turn towards it.

deep.x: Earth spins once on its axis every 23 hours 56 minutes relative to the stars, the "sidereal day". Because Earth also moves along its orbit, it needs an extra ~4 minutes to bring the Sun back to the same position: the 24-hour solar day.
How fast are we moving?

At the equator, Earth's surface spins at about 1,670 km/h. In Portugal, at about 40°N, it's around 1,280 km/h. We don't feel it because the motion is smooth and everything, including the air, moves with us.
Time zones

Since noon moves westward with the Sun, the world is divided into 24 time zones of roughly 15° each. Portugal's mainland uses Western European Time (UTC+0, +1 in summer), the Azores are an hour behind.
Twilight

After sunset the sky stays light because the atmosphere scatters sunlight from below the horizon. Twilight is shorter near the equator, where the Sun sets steeply, and lasts for hours in summer near the poles.
Earth's spin is slowly slowing because of the Moon's tides: days get about 2 milliseconds longer per century. 400 million years ago a year had about 400 days.

cards.title: Moon phases
cards.text: The Moon doesn't make light; it reflects sunlight. As it orbits Earth every 29.5 days, we see different amounts of its lit half.

deep.x: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun. Phases depend on how much of that lit half faces us. As the Moon orbits Earth every 29.5 days, the angle between Sun, Earth and Moon changes.

steps: New Moon: lit side faces away
Full Moon: lit side faces us

deep.x: Waxing or waning?

In the Northern Hemisphere, a Moon lit on the right is growing (waxing); lit on the left, it's shrinking (waning). A Portuguese saying: "a Lua é mentirosa", the Moon lies. When it's shaped like a C it's actually shrinking (decrescente), and when it's shaped like a D it's growing (crescente), the opposite of what the letters suggest.
When to see it

x: A full Moon rises at sunset and sets at sunrise
A first-quarter Moon is high at sunset
A waning crescent is only visible before dawn

deep.w: Phases are caused by Earth's shadow
deep.r: They're caused by our changing view of the sunlit half; Earth's shadow only matters in eclipses

deep.x: 27 or 29.5 days?
The Moon orbits in 27.3 days relative to the stars, but because Earth moves around the Sun meanwhile, it takes 29.5 days to return to the same phase.
The word "month" comes from "Moon": calendars across the world were based on its phases.

cards.title: The far side

items.r: the far side, which gets sunlight too

cards.text: The Moon always shows us the same face because it spins exactly once per orbit, known as tidal locking. The far side isn't dark; it gets as much sunlight as the near side.

deep.x: The Moon rotates once on its axis in exactly the time it takes to orbit Earth, so the same face always points towards us. This "tidal locking" happened because Earth's gravity raised bulges on the young Moon and braked its spin until the two periods matched.
Seeing a bit more
Thanks to slight wobbles called libration, we actually see about 59% of the Moon's surface over time, not just 50%.
A different face

The far side, first photographed by the Soviet Luna 3 in 1959, looks very different: heavily cratered, with almost none of the dark lava plains ("maria") that make the "face" on the near side. Its crust is thicker, which may have stopped lava reaching the surface.
Landing there
In 2019 China's Chang'e 4 made the first soft landing on the far side, using a relay satellite to talk to Earth. Chang'e 6 brought the first far-side samples home in 2024.

deep.w: The far side is always dark
deep.r: It gets day and night like the near side; it's just hidden from us

deep.x: Pink Floyd's "Dark Side of the Moon" is poetic but wrong: "far side" is the correct term.

cards.title: Solar eclipses
cards.text: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth. By coincidence, the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times further away, so they look the same size.

deep.x: A solar eclipse happens at new Moon, when the Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth. It doesn't happen every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° to Earth's; usually the Moon passes a little above or below the Sun.

steps: Lines up exactly with the Sun

deep.x: Types

items: Annular: Moon too far, ring of fire

deep.x: Totality

During a total eclipse, the sky darkens in minutes, temperatures drop, birds go quiet and the Sun's pearly corona appears. Totality lasts at most about 7.5 minutes and is visible only along a path ~100–200 km wide.
Iberia's eclipses
A total eclipse crosses northern Spain on 12 August 2026, with a partial eclipse across Portugal. Another total eclipse crosses southern Spain on 2 August 2027, with the Algarve close to the path.
The Moon is slowly moving away from Earth by about 3.8 cm a year. In roughly 600 million years it will look too small to cause total eclipses.
Never look at the Sun without certified eclipse glasses, except during the brief moment of totality itself.

cards.title: Lunar eclipses
cards.text: In a lunar eclipse, Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. The Moon turns coppery red because Earth's atmosphere bends red sunlight onto it.

deep.x: A lunar eclipse happens at full Moon, when Earth passes directly between the Sun and the Moon. Unlike solar eclipses, it can be seen from the whole night side of Earth, and it's perfectly safe to watch.
Why red?

Earth's atmosphere scatters blue light (that's why the sky is blue) and lets red light through. Sunlight passing through the atmosphere around Earth's edge is bent into the shadow, painting the Moon with the red glow of all the world's sunrises and sunsets at once.
Shadow parts

x: **Penumbra**: the faint outer shadow; the Moon dims only slightly
**Umbra**: the dark inner shadow; this is where the Moon turns red
Totality can last over an hour and a half

deep.x: A clue to Earth's shape
Aristotle noticed that Earth's shadow on the Moon is always round, whatever the angle: evidence that Earth is a sphere, more than 2,300 years ago.
After big volcanic eruptions, dust in the atmosphere makes lunar eclipses darker, sometimes making the Moon almost vanish.

cards.title: Tides
cards.text: The Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans, creating two bulges of water: one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side. As Earth turns, most coasts get two high tides a day.

deep.x: The Moon's gravity pulls more strongly on the side of Earth facing it than on Earth's centre, and more strongly on the centre than on the far side. These differences stretch the oceans into two bulges: one towards the Moon and one away from it.

steps: Moon's pull strongest on near side

deep.x: Spring and neap tides

The Sun also raises tides, about half as strong as the Moon's. When Sun and Moon line up (new and full Moon), their effects add up: spring tides, with the biggest range. At quarter Moons they partly cancel: neap tides.
Why the timing shifts
The Moon moves along its orbit as Earth turns, so it takes about 24 h 50 min to return overhead. That's why high tide is about 50 minutes later each day.
Local differences

x: Coastline shape amplifies tides: the Bay of Fundy in Canada reaches about 16 m
Portugal's Atlantic coast has a range of up to about 3.5–4 m at spring tides
The Mediterranean has tiny tides, often under 30 cm

deep.x: Tidal friction is slowly slowing Earth's spin and pushing the Moon away.

cards.title: Where the Moon came from
cards.text: The leading theory: about 4.5 billion years ago, a Mars-sized body called Theia crashed into the young Earth, and the debris came together to form the Moon.

deep.x: The giant-impact theory says that about 4.5 billion years ago, a Mars-sized protoplanet, named Theia, struck the young Earth a glancing blow. Molten rock and vapour blasted into orbit and clumped together, perhaps within years, into the Moon.
The evidence

x: Apollo rocks have almost the same oxygen isotopes as Earth's mantle
The Moon has a small iron core, as expected if it formed from outer layers
Lunar rocks are depleted in easily evaporated elements, as if heated intensely
Computer simulations reproduce the Earth–Moon system

deep.x: Open questions

The Moon's composition is almost too similar to Earth's: if Theia was a different body, why aren't its traces more obvious? Some models suggest a more violent collision that thoroughly mixed both bodies.
The Moon's importance
The Moon stabilises Earth's tilt, keeping seasons and climate relatively steady over millions of years. Without it, the tilt could wobble wildly.
When it formed, the Moon was perhaps 15 times closer than today, appearing enormous in the sky.

cards.title: Shooting stars
cards.text: Meteors are specks of dust burning up in the atmosphere at tens of km per second. Meteor showers like the Perseids (August) happen when Earth crosses a comet's trail.

deep.x: A meteor is a flash of light made by a grain of dust or rock, often smaller than a grain of sand, hitting the atmosphere at 11–72 km/s. It's not burning like fire: compressing air in front of it heats it, and it vaporises, making the air glow.
Meteor showers
Comets leave trails of dust along their orbits. When Earth crosses one, many meteors appear to come from one point in the sky, the radiant, which names the shower.
Watching tips

x: Go somewhere dark, lie back and let your eyes adapt for 20 minutes
The best hours are after midnight, when your side of Earth faces "forward" into the debris
No telescope needed: they streak across the whole sky

v.unit: meteors per hour at peak, dark sky

deep.x: Meteorites
About 50 tonnes of space dust and rock fall on Earth every day, mostly as dust. Meteorites that survive are prized: some are 4.6 billion years old, older than any Earth rock.
Swift–Tuttle, the comet behind the Perseids, is about 26 km wide, more than twice the size of the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs. Its orbit is being watched.

cards.title: Spotting planets

items: Jupiter: bright all night when visible

cards.text: Planets don't twinkle as much as stars and move slowly against the background over weeks. Venus is often the brightest "star" right after sunset or before dawn.

deep.x: Stars twinkle because they're points of light, easily jostled by moving air. Planets are tiny discs, so their light is steadier. Planets also wander against the background stars over days and weeks, always staying near the Sun's path, the ecliptic.
The five naked-eye planets

x: **Venus**: the brightest, never far from the Sun; "evening star" or "morning star"
**Jupiter**: very bright, visible much of the night when well placed
**Mars**: distinctly orange-red; very bright every ~26 months
**Saturn**: steady yellowish; its rings need a small telescope
**Mercury**: hard to catch, low in twilight

deep.x: With binoculars
Steady binoculars show Jupiter's four big moons as tiny dots that move from night to night, just as Galileo saw them in 1610. Venus shows phases like the Moon through a small telescope.
Free apps like Stellarium show where each planet is tonight from your location.
Venus can be bright enough to cast faint shadows on a truly dark night.

quiz.q: What causes the seasons?
quiz.explain: The tilt changes the angle of sunlight.

quiz.q: Why does the Moon look red in a lunar eclipse?
options: Earth's atmosphere bends red light onto it
quiz.explain: Like all the sunsets on Earth at once.

lessons.title: Life in the universe
lessons.summary: Exoplanets, aliens and the big questions.

cards.title: Exoplanets
cards.text: An exoplanet orbits a star other than the Sun. The first around a Sun-like star was found in 1995; today more than 5,000 are confirmed.

deep.x: For centuries, people wondered whether other stars had planets. The first confirmed exoplanets, found in 1992, orbited a pulsar, a dead star. In 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found 51 Pegasi b, a giant planet orbiting a Sun-like star every 4 days, winning the 2019 Nobel Prize.
A zoo of worlds

items: Hot Jupiters: giants close to their star
Rogue planets: no star at all

deep.x: Statistics

Kepler's survey suggests most stars have planets, and there are likely more planets than stars in the Milky Way. Super-Earths and mini-Neptunes, which don't exist in our Solar System, are the most common types.
Famous systems

x: **TRAPPIST-1**: seven Earth-sized planets around a red dwarf 40 light-years away
**Proxima b**: a planet in the habitable zone of the nearest star
**Kepler-16b**: orbits two suns, like Tatooine

deep.x: Our Solar System, with small rocky planets inside and giants outside, may not be typical at all.

cards.title: Finding them

steps: A planet is passing in front

cards.text: Most exoplanets are found by the transit method: when a planet passes in front of its star, the star dims slightly and regularly.

deep.x: Planets are tiny and faint next to their stars, so most are found indirectly, by their effect on the star.

items: Direct imaging: photo of the planet
Microlensing: gravity magnifies a background star

deep.x: Transits

When a planet crosses in front of its star, it blocks a small fraction of the light. Jupiter would dim the Sun by about 1%; Earth by only 0.008%. Repeated, regular dips reveal the planet's size and orbit.
Radial velocity

A planet and its star orbit a shared centre, so the star wobbles. Its light shifts slightly blue as it approaches and red as it recedes. Earth makes the Sun wobble by only about 9 cm/s, walking pace for a snail.
Combining methods
Transits give a planet's size; radial velocity gives its mass. Together they give density, telling us whether it's rocky, watery or gassy.
Webb can analyse starlight filtering through a transiting planet's atmosphere and has detected water vapour, CO₂ and methane on distant worlds.

cards.title: The Goldilocks zone
cards.text: The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where it's neither too hot nor too cold for liquid water on a planet's surface.

deep.x: The habitable zone is the range of orbits where a planet with an atmosphere could keep liquid water on its surface. Its location depends on the star: close in for cool red dwarfs, farther out for hot stars.
Our Solar System's zone
The Sun's habitable zone spans roughly from just outside Venus to around Mars. Earth sits comfortably inside; Mars is near the outer edge but too small to hold a thick atmosphere.
It's not that simple

x: Atmosphere matters: Venus would be habitable distance-wise if it lacked its greenhouse
Moons outside the zone, like Europa, may have oceans heated by tides
Planets need a magnetic field and time for life to develop

deep.w: Habitable zone means a planet has life
deep.r: It only means liquid water is possible on the surface

deep.x: The zone moves
As stars age, they brighten, and the habitable zone moves outwards. In about a billion years, Earth will drift out of the inner edge.
Many scientists prefer "temperate zone": "habitable" promises more than we know.

cards.title: What life needs
cards.text: Life as we know it needs liquid water, an energy source and chemistry built around carbon. On Earth, microbes live in boiling springs, ice and deep rock.

deep.x: Every living thing we know needs liquid water as a solvent, a source of energy (sunlight or chemical reactions) and chemistry built mainly from carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulphur, often remembered as CHNOPS.
Why carbon and water?

Carbon forms four bonds and long, stable chains: perfect for complex molecules like DNA. Water stays liquid over a wide temperature range, dissolves many substances and floats when frozen, insulating lakes below.
Life at the edges
Earth's extremophiles expand the possibilities: microbes thrive in boiling vents, Antarctic ice, acid pools, nuclear reactor water and kilometres down in solid rock.
Biosignatures

To find life elsewhere, scientists look for chemical signs that are hard to explain without biology, such as oxygen and methane together in an atmosphere, which react and would vanish unless constantly replenished.
Life on Earth appeared within a few hundred million years of the planet cooling: a hint that it may arise easily where conditions allow.

cards.title: Places to look nearby
cards.text: Mars may once have had rivers; Jupiter's moon Europa and Saturn's moon Enceladus have oceans under their ice, and Enceladus sprays water into space.

deep.x: Our best chances to find life beyond Earth may be in our own Solar System, where spacecraft can visit and sample.

items: Titan: methane lakes and an inner ocean

deep.x: Mars
Mars had lakes, rivers and a thicker atmosphere over 3 billion years ago. Perseverance is collecting samples from an ancient lake bed; any life today would likely be microbial, underground.
Enceladus

Cassini flew through plumes of water erupting from cracks at Enceladus' south pole and found salts, silica and organic molecules: signs of a salty ocean in contact with hot rock, much like Earth's hydrothermal vents.
Europa and Titan

x: Europa Clipper (launched 2024) will study Europa's ocean from orbit from 2030
Dragonfly, a nuclear-powered drone, is planned to fly across Titan in the 2030s
Titan's lakes of methane could host very different chemistry

deep.x: Enceladus is only about 500 km wide, about the length of mainland Portugal, yet it may have one of the most promising oceans for life.

cards.title: The Drake equation

viz.f: N = R* · fp · ne · fl · fi · fc · L

cards.text: In 1961 Frank Drake listed the factors needed to estimate how many civilisations might be signalling in our galaxy. Most of the numbers are still unknown.

deep.x: Frank Drake wrote his equation for the first SETI meeting in 1961. It isn't meant to be solved exactly but to organise our ignorance: it breaks a big question into smaller ones we can study.

v.f: N = R* · fp · ne · fl · fi · fc · L

deep.x: What we've learnt
Since 1961, astronomers have measured the first factors: stars form at a few per year, and nearly all have planets, many in habitable zones. The biological and social factors remain complete guesses.
Wildly different answers

Plug in optimistic guesses and you get millions of civilisations; pessimistic ones give less than one. The lifetime L dominates: if civilisations broadcast for only a century, we'd have little overlap with any.
The equation's real value is showing which questions matter: how often life starts, and how long technological civilisations last.

cards.title: The Fermi paradox
cards.text: If the galaxy is old and huge, why haven't we met anyone? Possible answers: life is rare, civilisations don't last, distances are too vast, or we're not looking the right way.

deep.x: In 1950, over lunch at Los Alamos, physicist Enrico Fermi asked, "Where is everybody?" Even with slow rockets, a civilisation could spread across the galaxy in a few million years, tiny compared with its 13-billion-year age. So why no sign of anyone?
Proposed answers

x: **Rare Earth**: complex life needs a rare combination of conditions
**Great Filter**: some step, early or late, almost always fails
**Short-lived civilisations**: they destroy themselves or fade quickly
**Too far, too slow**: signals are weak and travel takes too long
**Zoo hypothesis**: they know we're here but stay hidden

deep.x: Why it matters
If the filter is behind us, life may be rare and we're lucky. If it's ahead, civilisations like ours may tend to end early: a sobering reason to manage risks wisely.

deep.w: Silence proves no one is out there
deep.r: We've searched a tiny fraction of stars and frequencies

deep.x: Astronomer Jill Tarter compared our search so far to scooping one glass of water from the ocean and concluding there are no fish.

cards.title: SETI
cards.text: The Search for Extra-Terrestrial Intelligence listens for radio signals from other civilisations. The famous 1977 "Wow! signal" was never detected again.

deep.x: SETI looks for "technosignatures": signs of technology rather than biology. Radio is the favourite medium because it crosses the galaxy easily, and a narrow-band signal, concentrated at one frequency, would stand out from natural noise.
The Wow! signal

On 15 August 1977, the Big Ear telescope in Ohio detected a strong narrow-band signal lasting 72 seconds. Astronomer Jerry Ehman circled it and wrote "Wow!" in the margin. It was never seen again, and its origin is still debated.
Modern searches

x: **Breakthrough Listen** (from 2016) surveys a million nearby stars and 100 galaxies
Searches now include laser flashes and infrared heat from huge structures
Citizen scientists once lent their home computers to SETI@home (1999–2020)

deep.x: False alarms
Pulsars were first nicknamed "LGM" (little green men) in 1967 because their pulses were so regular. In 2019 a promising signal turned out to be human-made interference.
The odds are long, but the payoff would be the most important discovery in history.

cards.title: Messages we sent
cards.text: In 1974 the Arecibo radio telescope beamed a message towards a star cluster 25,000 light-years away. The Voyager golden records carry greetings in 55 languages.

deep.x: Humanity has sent a few deliberate messages into space, designed to be understood without a shared language: through mathematics, physics and pictures.
The Arecibo message

Written by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan, it was 1,679 bits long, a product of two primes (23 × 73) so it could be arranged into a grid. The picture shows numbers 1–10, DNA's elements, a human figure, the Solar System and the telescope.

x: 1,679 bits
arrange in a 23 × 73 grid

deep.x: The Pioneer plaques
Pioneer 10 and 11 carry plaques showing a man and woman, the Solar System and the Sun's position relative to 14 pulsars, which work like a cosmic map.
Should we shout?

Some scientists argue against "messaging extraterrestrial intelligence" (METI) until we know more: if others exist, announcing ourselves may be unwise. Others say our radio leakage has been spreading for a century anyway.
The Arecibo message is aimed at globular cluster M13, 25,000 light-years away; by the time it arrives, the cluster will have moved.

cards.title: The pale blue dot
cards.text: In 1990, Voyager 1 photographed Earth from about 6 billion km away: a speck of light less than a pixel wide. Carl Sagan used it to remind us how small and precious our world is.

deep.x: On 14 February 1990, just before its cameras were switched off, Voyager 1 turned around and took a "family portrait" of the planets from about 6 billion km away. Earth appeared as a pale blue speck, 0.12 pixels wide, caught in a sunbeam scattered in the camera.
Sagan's reflection

Carl Sagan had pushed NASA to take the photo. In his 1994 book he wrote that every human who ever lived, "every saint and sinner", lived on that mote of dust, and that it underscores our responsibility to treat each other kindly and preserve our only home.
Other famous Earth portraits
The overview effect
Astronauts often describe a shift in perspective when seeing Earth from space: borders vanish and the thin atmosphere looks fragile. Images like these helped inspire the environmental movement.
From far enough away, all human history fits inside a single pixel.

lessons.title: Mars, the red planet
lessons.summary: Our most explored neighbour.

cards.title: Why it's red
cards.text: Mars is red because its dust is rich in iron oxide: rust. The fine dust gets everywhere, even tinting the sky a butterscotch colour.

deep.x: Mars' surface is covered in fine dust rich in iron oxide, the same compound as rust. Over billions of years, iron in volcanic rocks reacted with small amounts of oxygen and water, and the planet literally rusted. Below the top layer, many rocks are darker grey or black basalt.

steps: Reacts with traces of oxygen and water

deep.x: A butterscotch sky
Dust suspended in the thin air scatters red light, so the daytime sky looks pinkish-tan. At sunset the opposite happens: fine dust scatters blue light forwards, and Martian sunsets glow blue.
The dust itself

x: Particles are tiny, around 3 micrometres, finer than flour
The dust is electrostatic and sticks to solar panels and spacesuits
It contains perchlorates, salts that are toxic to humans: a challenge for future crews

deep.x: The ancient Romans named Mars after their god of war because of its blood-red colour; the Greeks called it Ares.

cards.title: A small, cold world
cards.text: Mars is about half Earth's width with roughly a third of its gravity. The average temperature is around −65 °C, and the air is 100 times thinner than ours.

deep.x: Mars is 6,779 km wide, about 53% of Earth's diameter, with only about 11% of Earth's mass. Its gravity is 38% of ours: a 70 kg person would feel like 27 kg.
Thin air

The atmosphere is 95% carbon dioxide, but so thin, about 0.6% of Earth's sea-level pressure, that water can't stay liquid on the surface: it boils or freezes. Unprotected, a human's blood would boil at body temperature.

v.unit: air pressure, % of Earth sea level

deep.x: Wild temperature swings

With thin air holding little heat, temperatures swing widely: near the equator a summer day can reach about +20 °C at noon and plunge to −70 °C at night. Polar winters drop below −120 °C, cold enough to freeze CO₂ into dry-ice snow.
Why Mars lost its air
Mars has no global magnetic field. Without that shield, the solar wind gradually stripped its atmosphere over billions of years, measured directly by NASA's MAVEN orbiter.
Small planets cool faster: Mars' smaller size is probably why its core and magnetic field died early.

cards.title: Day and year
cards.text: A Martian day, called a sol, lasts 24 h 37 min, very close to ours. A Martian year is 687 Earth days, so its seasons last about twice as long.

deep.x: A Martian solar day, called a sol, lasts 24 hours 39 minutes. Mission controllers living on "Mars time" shift their schedule by about 40 minutes every day, which is famously exhausting.
Seasons

Mars' axis is tilted 25°, similar to Earth's 23.4°, so it has seasons too. But its orbit is more elliptical, so seasons are uneven: southern summers are shorter and hotter, and they often trigger dust storms.
Seasons in numbers

x: Polar ice caps grow and shrink with the seasons as CO₂ freezes and evaporates
About a quarter of Mars' atmosphere freezes onto the poles in winter

deep.x: Mars' tilt isn't stabilised by a large moon, so over millions of years it wobbles between roughly 15° and 45°, causing big climate shifts.

cards.title: Olympus Mons
cards.text: Mars has the tallest volcano in the Solar System: Olympus Mons, about 22 km high, two and a half times the height of Everest, and about 600 km wide, roughly the length of Portugal.

deep.x: Olympus Mons is a shield volcano, built by countless eruptions of runny lava, like Hawaii's volcanoes but vastly bigger. It rises about 22 km above the surrounding plains and covers an area roughly the size of Poland.
Why so big?

x: **No plate tectonics**: on Earth, plates move over hotspots, creating chains of smaller volcanoes; on Mars, the crust stays put, so lava piles up in one place
**Lower gravity**: allows taller structures before they collapse
**Long life**: eruptions may have continued for billions of years

deep.x: Standing on it

Its slopes are so gentle, about 5°, that standing on the summit you couldn't see it was a mountain: the horizon on Mars is close, and the volcano's edges would be far beyond it. Its summit caldera is about 80 km wide.
Olympus Mons is ringed by cliffs up to 8 km high, taller than Everest.

cards.title: Valles Marineris
cards.text: A canyon system about 4,000 km long and up to 7 km deep cuts across Mars. On Earth it would stretch roughly from Lisbon to Moscow.

deep.x: Valles Marineris is a system of canyons about 4,000 km long, up to 200 km wide and 7 km deep. It would span the continental United States or stretch roughly from Lisbon to Moscow.
Not carved by a river

Unlike the Grand Canyon, Valles Marineris formed mainly as the crust cracked and pulled apart, probably when the nearby Tharsis volcanic region bulged upwards. Later, landslides and possibly water widened it.
Named after a spacecraft
It's named after Mariner 9, the first spacecraft to orbit another planet, in 1971. When it arrived, a global dust storm hid everything except the tops of the giant volcanoes.

x: Layered rocks on its walls record billions of years of Martian history
Some areas show minerals that formed in water

deep.x: On Earth the closest comparison is the East African Rift, also formed by the crust pulling apart.

cards.title: Water on Mars
cards.text: Dry riverbeds, deltas and minerals that form in water show Mars once had lakes and rivers. Today water survives as ice at the poles and underground.

deep.x: The evidence that Mars was once wet is overwhelming: dry river valleys, deltas, lake beds, and minerals like clays and sulphates that only form in water. Curiosity found ancient lake sediments in Gale Crater; Perseverance landed on a river delta in Jezero Crater.
Where's the water now?

x: Frozen in the polar ice caps; the south cap alone could cover Mars in water about 11 m deep
Buried as ice just below the surface across large regions
Some lost to space as the atmosphere thinned
Possibly locked in minerals or deep underground

deep.x: Liquid water today?

Pure liquid water can't last on the surface, but salty brines may form briefly. In 2024 seismic data from the InSight lander suggested a deep reservoir of liquid water 10–20 km down, too deep to reach easily.

deep.w: Mars has always been a dry desert
deep.r: It once had lakes, rivers and perhaps a northern ocean

deep.x: If life ever started on Mars, the wet era over 3.5 billion years ago is when it most likely happened.

cards.title: Two tiny moons
cards.text: Mars has two small, lumpy moons, Phobos and Deimos, probably captured asteroids or debris from an impact. Phobos is slowly spiralling inwards.

deep.x: Phobos (fear) and Deimos (dread), named after the sons of the Greek war god, were discovered in 1877 by Asaph Hall. They're small, dark and potato-shaped, more like asteroids than our round Moon.
Phobos' doom

Phobos orbits only about 6,000 km above Mars' surface, closer than any other moon to its planet, and it's spiralling inwards by about 2 m per century. In 30–50 million years it will either crash into Mars or be torn apart into a ring.
Where did they come from?

They may be captured asteroids, but their orbits are neat circles above the equator, which fits better with formation from debris after a giant impact, like our Moon. Japan's MMX mission aims to bring samples from Phobos to settle the question.
From Mars, Phobos rises in the west and sets in the east twice a day, because it orbits faster than Mars spins.

cards.title: Dust storms
cards.text: Mars has dust storms that can cover the whole planet for weeks. A 2018 storm ended the Opportunity rover's mission by blocking sunlight to its solar panels.

deep.x: Mars' dust storms are driven by sunlight heating dust, which warms the air, which lifts more dust: a feedback loop. Local storms are common; every few Martian years, they merge into planet-wide storms lasting months.

steps: Air rises and winds pick up

deep.x: Not like the film

Martian winds can be fast, but the air is so thin that a 100 km/h gust would feel like a light breeze. The dramatic storm that strands the astronaut in *The Martian* couldn't really knock over equipment.

deep.w: Mars storms can blow over rockets
deep.r: Thin air means even fast winds push very gently

deep.x: Real dangers

x: Dust blocks sunlight, starving solar-powered machines (Opportunity, 2018)
Fine dust gets into seals, joints and lungs
Storms change temperatures and the atmosphere's structure

deep.x: Dust devils
Whirlwinds of dust, some kilometres tall, sweep across the plains, leaving dark tracks. They sometimes helpfully cleaned rovers' solar panels.
Future crews will likely prefer nuclear power, which works day and night through any storm.

cards.title: Getting there
cards.text: Launch windows to Mars open about every 26 months, when the planets line up. The trip takes six to nine months.

deep.x: Earth and Mars orbit at different speeds, so the distance between them varies from about 55 million km to 400 million km. Spacecraft use a "Hohmann transfer": an efficient half-ellipse that leaves Earth and meets Mars on the far side of the Sun.
Launch windows
Efficient alignments come every 26 months, so missions cluster: in 2020, NASA, China and the UAE all launched to Mars within weeks.
Landing is hard

The "seven minutes of terror": a lander enters at about 20,000 km/h and must stop within minutes, using a heat shield, parachute and rockets. The thin air is too thin for parachutes alone but thick enough to burn up. About half of all Mars missions have failed.
Because of the radio delay of up to 24 minutes, landings are fully automatic: by the time engineers hear the craft has entered the atmosphere, it has already landed or crashed.

cards.title: Living on Mars?
cards.text: Humans on Mars would need shelter from radiation and cold, oxygen made from CO₂, and water dug from ice. It's possible, but far harder than living in Antarctica.

deep.x: Mars is the most Earth-like planet nearby, but it's still extremely hostile. Every human necessity, air, water, food, warmth and protection, would have to be engineered.

items.b: made from CO₂ (MOXIE did it in 2021)

deep.x: Radiation
Without a magnetic field or thick air, Mars' surface gets about 40–50 times Earth's background radiation. Habitats would likely be covered by metres of soil or built in lava tubes.
Living off the land
NASA's MOXIE experiment on Perseverance proved oxygen can be extracted from Martian CO₂. The same chemistry could produce rocket fuel for the trip home, a key idea called in-situ resource use.
Health and psychology

x: Muscle and bone loss in low gravity, though 38% may help compared with zero
Isolation, with no quick way home and delayed messages
Analogue missions in Antarctica, Hawaii and deserts test crews for years

deep.x: Even the hardest places on Earth, like Antarctica in winter, are easier than Mars: you can breathe the air.
