lessons.title: Giant planets and their moons
lessons.summary: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune and their worlds.

cards.title: Gas and ice giants
cards.text: Jupiter and Saturn are mostly hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune have more water, ammonia and methane "ices", which is why they're called ice giants.

deep.x: The giant planets formed beyond the "frost line", where ice was abundant. Jupiter and Saturn grew cores big enough fast enough to capture vast hydrogen envelopes. Uranus and Neptune formed later or farther out, where material was sparser, so they captured less gas.

items: Dense core of rock and ice

deep.x: Inside the two kinds
Colours
Jupiter's bands come from ammonia clouds and unknown colouring compounds. Uranus and Neptune look blue-green because methane in their air absorbs red light.
Diamond rain?

Inside Uranus and Neptune, extreme pressure may break methane apart and squeeze the carbon into diamonds that sink slowly towards the core. Lab experiments with lasers have produced tiny diamonds under similar conditions.
Many known exoplanets are "mini-Neptunes", so understanding our own ice giants helps explain worlds across the galaxy.

cards.title: Jupiter's protection?
cards.text: Jupiter's huge gravity flings or captures many comets and asteroids. It may shield the inner planets, though it can also send some our way.

deep.x: The popular idea is that Jupiter acts as a cosmic shield, catching or flinging away comets that would otherwise hit Earth. Reality is more mixed: simulations show Jupiter also nudges asteroids and comets into the inner Solar System.
Impacts on Jupiter

In 1994 comet Shoemaker–Levy 9, torn into 21 pieces by Jupiter's gravity, crashed into the planet over six days. The impacts left dark scars larger than Earth, watched by telescopes worldwide. Amateur astronomers still catch small flashes of impacts.
Shaping the Solar System

x: Jupiter's gravity stopped a planet forming in the asteroid belt
It may have migrated inwards and back out early on (the "Grand Tack"), keeping Mars small
Its resonances create gaps in the asteroid belt (Kirkwood gaps)

deep.x: Jupiter is less a bodyguard than a traffic controller: it shapes where small bodies go, for better and worse.

cards.title: Io, the volcanic moon
cards.text: Jupiter's moon Io is the most volcanic place known, with hundreds of volcanoes. Jupiter's gravity squeezes it like a stress ball, heating its interior.

deep.x: Io, slightly bigger than our Moon, is the most volcanically active body known, with over 400 active volcanoes. Some fountain sulphur plumes up to 400 km high; lava lakes are hotter than Earth's lavas.
Tidal heating

Io's orbit is slightly oval because Europa and Ganymede tug on it rhythmically. As Io moves closer and farther from Jupiter, its rocky body flexes by up to about 100 m, generating heat by friction like bending a paperclip back and forth.
The resonance
A colourful world
Sulphur compounds paint Io yellow, orange, red and white, giving it the look of a pizza. It has almost no impact craters, because lava resurfaces it constantly.
Linda Morabito discovered Io's volcanoes in 1979 while processing Voyager images for navigation: she noticed a strange bump on the moon's edge.

cards.title: Europa's ocean
cards.text: Under Europa's icy crust lies a salty ocean with perhaps twice the water of all Earth's oceans. NASA's Europa Clipper, launched in 2024, will study it.

deep.x: Europa, slightly smaller than our Moon, has a smooth icy crust criss-crossed by cracks and ridges. Beneath an ice shell perhaps 15–25 km thick lies a global salty ocean around 60–150 km deep, kept liquid by tidal heating.
Evidence for an ocean

x: Galileo detected a magnetic signal consistent with a salty, conductive ocean
Few craters: the surface is young and constantly renewed
"Chaos terrain" looks like icebergs that broke, shifted and refroze
Hubble and Webb spotted possible water plumes and surface CO₂

deep.x: Why it's exciting
The ocean is in contact with rock, which could supply chemical energy like Earth's deep-sea vents. Water, energy and chemistry are the three ingredients for life.
Europa Clipper

Launched in October 2024, Europa Clipper will make about 50 flybys from 2030, measuring the ice thickness, ocean saltiness and surface chemistry. It's the largest planetary spacecraft NASA has built, with solar panels over 30 m across.
Europa probably holds about twice as much liquid water as all of Earth's oceans combined.

cards.title: Ganymede
cards.text: Ganymede, another moon of Jupiter, is the largest moon in the Solar System, bigger than the planet Mercury, and has its own magnetic field.

deep.x: Ganymede is 5,268 km wide, bigger than Mercury, though only half its mass because it's made largely of ice. It's the only moon known to generate its own magnetic field, which creates small auroras around it.
A layered world
Ganymede likely has an iron core, a rocky mantle, and thick ice layers sandwiching a salty ocean that may hold more water than Earth's oceans.
Two kinds of terrain

x: Dark, ancient regions heavily cratered
Lighter, grooved terrain where the ice was cracked and resurfaced

deep.x: ESA's JUICE
The JUpiter ICy moons Explorer, launched in 2023, will arrive in 2031 and later become the first spacecraft to orbit a moon other than ours: Ganymede.
Galileo discovered Ganymede in 1610; it was named after a Trojan prince carried off by Zeus.

cards.title: Titan
cards.text: Saturn's moon Titan has a thick orange atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane and ethane. The Huygens probe landed there in 2005.

deep.x: Titan, Saturn's largest moon, is the only moon with a thick atmosphere, about 1.5 times Earth's surface pressure, mostly nitrogen. At −179 °C, methane plays the role water plays on Earth: it forms clouds, rain, rivers, lakes and seas.
Huygens' landing
In January 2005 ESA's Huygens probe parachuted through the orange haze for 2.5 hours and landed on a damp plain strewn with rounded "pebbles" of water ice: the most distant landing ever made.
Lakes and seas
Kraken Mare, the largest sea, is bigger than the Caspian Sea. Waves are rare and the liquid is clear enough that Cassini's radar saw to the bottom in places.
Dragonfly
NASA's Dragonfly, a car-sized nuclear-powered drone, is planned to launch in 2028 and fly between sites on Titan in the 2030s, studying prebiotic chemistry.
With low gravity and thick air, a human on Titan could fly by flapping strapped-on wings.

cards.title: Saturn floats
cards.text: Saturn's average density is lower than water's. Given a big enough bathtub, it would float, although it's a ball of gas, not a solid.

deep.x: Saturn's average density is about 0.69 g/cm³, less than water's 1 g/cm³. It's mostly hydrogen and helium, the lightest elements. Of course, no bathtub is big enough, and Saturn would dissolve rather than bob, but the comparison shows how light it is.
Flattened by spin
Saturn spins once every 10.7 hours. Combined with its low density, that makes it the most flattened planet: its equator is about 10% wider than its pole-to-pole diameter.
The hexagon
At Saturn's north pole, a jet stream forms a six-sided pattern, each side wider than Earth. It's a stable wave pattern in the atmosphere and has lasted at least since Voyager saw it in 1981.
Many moons
Saturn has the most known moons of any planet, over 270, mostly small irregular ones captured long ago.

x: Titan: thick atmosphere
Enceladus: water plumes
Mimas: a giant crater that makes it look like the Death Star
Iapetus: one side dark, one side bright

deep.x: Saturn radiates more heat than it receives from the Sun, partly because helium "rain" sinks inside it and releases energy.

cards.title: Uranus on its side
cards.text: Uranus is tilted about 98°, so it rolls around the Sun on its side. Each pole gets 42 years of continuous daylight and then 42 years of night.

deep.x: Uranus is tilted about 98°, so its axis lies almost in the plane of its orbit. It likely suffered one or more huge collisions early in its history that knocked it over.
Extreme seasons
During one part of its orbit, a pole points almost straight at the Sun; half an orbit later, it points away. Each pole gets about 42 years of daylight followed by 42 years of darkness.

events.l: Voyager 2 sees the south pole facing the Sun

deep.x: Discovery

William Herschel found Uranus in 1781 with a homemade telescope, the first planet discovered since antiquity. He wanted to name it after King George III ("Georgium Sidus"); astronomers chose Uranus, father of Saturn.
Mysteries

x: Uranus barely emits more heat than it receives, unlike the other giants
Its magnetic field is tilted 59° and offset from the centre
It has 13 faint rings and 28 known moons named after Shakespeare and Pope characters

deep.x: Scientists have ranked a dedicated Uranus orbiter as a top priority for the coming decades.

cards.title: Neptune's winds
cards.text: Neptune, the farthest planet, has the fastest winds in the Solar System, above 2,000 km/h. It was found in 1846 by mathematics before anyone saw it.

deep.x: Neptune has the fastest winds measured in the Solar System, up to about 2,100 km/h, despite receiving only 1/900th of the sunlight Earth does. The energy likely comes from heat escaping its interior.
Discovered with maths

Astronomers noticed Uranus drifting from its predicted path. Urbain Le Verrier calculated where an unseen planet must be pulling it. On 23 September 1846, Johann Galle pointed a telescope there and found Neptune within 1° of the prediction.
Triton

Neptune's largest moon, Triton, orbits backwards, a sign it was captured, probably from the Kuiper Belt. Voyager 2 saw geysers of nitrogen erupting from its frozen surface. Tides are slowly dragging it inwards.

x: Neptune completed its first full orbit since discovery only in 2011
The Great Dark Spot seen in 1989 later vanished, and new spots have appeared

deep.x: Galileo actually saw Neptune in 1612 and 1613, but thought it was a star.

cards.title: Visits to the giants
cards.text: Only Voyager 2 has visited Uranus and Neptune, in 1986 and 1989. Galileo and Juno studied Jupiter; Cassini orbited Saturn for 13 years.

deep.x: Every close look at the outer planets has come from a handful of robotic spacecraft. Their flybys and orbits transformed points of light into worlds.
Cassini's grand finale

After 13 years at Saturn, nearly out of fuel, Cassini dived between the planet and its rings 22 times, then plunged into Saturn's atmosphere in September 2017. Burning it up ensured it could never contaminate Enceladus or Titan.
What they found
Why so few?
Missions to the outer planets are long (years to decades) and need nuclear power, because sunlight is weak far from the Sun. Each one is a once-in-a-generation project.
Voyager 2 remains the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus and Neptune, almost 40 years ago.

lessons.title: The Sun up close
lessons.summary: Our star and its moods.

cards.title: Layers of the Sun
cards.text: Energy is made in the core, then crawls outwards through the radiative zone over tens of thousands of years, bubbles up through the convective zone and escapes from the surface.

deep.x: The Sun has no solid surface. Its structure is defined by how energy moves outward from the core.
The slow escape

In the radiative zone, a photon of light is absorbed and re-emitted countless times in random directions. This "random walk" means energy takes from about 10,000 to 170,000 years to cross it. Then, in the convective zone, hot plasma rises like boiling soup, carrying energy to the surface in weeks.

steps: Random walk through radiative zone, ~100,000 years

deep.x: Granulation
The photosphere looks grainy in close-up: granules around 1,000 km wide, about twice the length of Portugal, the tops of convection cells, each lasting about 8–20 minutes before being replaced.

x: Core: about a quarter of the Sun's radius, where almost all fusion happens
Density at the core is about 150 times that of water

deep.x: We can "see" inside the Sun with helioseismology: tracking sound waves that make its surface ripple, much as earthquakes reveal Earth's interior.

cards.title: Hot and hotter
cards.text: The surface is about 5,500 °C, but the outer atmosphere, the corona, reaches over a million degrees. Why it's so hot is still being studied.

deep.x: Moving away from a heater, it gets colder. But above the Sun's 5,500 °C surface, the temperature rises dramatically: the thin corona reaches 1–3 million °C. This "coronal heating problem" has puzzled scientists since the 1940s.
Leading explanations

x: **Nanoflares**: countless tiny magnetic explosions continuously heating the corona
**Waves**: magnetic waves carrying energy up from below and dissipating
Parker Solar Probe and Solar Orbiter are testing both by flying close

deep.x: Hot but not dense
The corona is extremely thin, so even at millions of degrees it holds little heat energy. You'd freeze before you'd cook, if the Sun's light didn't get you first.
Seeing the corona
The corona is normally hidden by the bright surface. It appears during a total solar eclipse as pearly streamers, or with coronagraphs, telescopes that block the Sun's disc.
Temperature measures how fast particles move, not how much heat they carry; the corona's particles are fast but few.

cards.title: Sunspots
cards.text: Sunspots are cooler, darker patches where magnetic fields block heat. Their numbers rise and fall over an 11-year solar cycle.

deep.x: Sunspots appear where intense magnetic fields poke through the surface and block the upward flow of heat. They're about 1,500 °C cooler than their surroundings, so they look dark, although on their own they'd glow brightly.
The 11-year cycle
Sunspot numbers rise and fall roughly every 11 years. At each solar maximum, the Sun's magnetic poles flip. Solar Cycle 25 peaked around 2024–25, producing strong auroras.
Size
Big sunspots can be several times wider than Earth. Groups often come in pairs with opposite magnetic polarity, like the ends of a bar magnet poking out.
The Maunder Minimum
From about 1645 to 1715, sunspots almost vanished. This coincided with part of the "Little Ice Age", though volcanic eruptions and other factors also played a role.
Galileo used sunspots to show that the Sun rotates and is not a perfect, unchanging sphere.
Never look at sunspots directly; use projection or a certified solar filter.

cards.title: Solar flares
cards.text: Flares are sudden bursts of energy from tangled magnetic fields. Big ones can disrupt radio, GPS and satellites on Earth.

deep.x: A flare happens when twisted magnetic field lines above sunspots suddenly snap and reconnect, releasing energy equal to millions of hydrogen bombs in minutes. Flares emit X-rays and ultraviolet light that reach Earth in about 8 minutes.
Flare classes
Coronal mass ejections

Flares often come with coronal mass ejections (CMEs): billions of tonnes of plasma hurled into space at hundreds to thousands of km/s. A CME takes 1–3 days to reach Earth, and it's the CME, not the flare, that drives big geomagnetic storms.
Effects on Earth

x: Radio blackouts for aircraft and ships
GPS errors and satellite damage
Extra drag that can bring satellites down early: in 2022, about 38 new satellites were lost after a storm
Higher radiation on polar flights

deep.x: The strongest flare ever recorded, in November 2003, saturated the sensors measuring it; it was later estimated at around X28 to X45.

cards.title: Solar wind
cards.text: The Sun constantly blows charged particles into space at around 400 km/s. Earth's magnetic field deflects most of them.

deep.x: The corona is so hot that the Sun's gravity can't hold it: it streams away as the solar wind, a constant flow of electrons and protons. The slow wind travels at about 400 km/s; the fast wind, from coronal holes, at about 750 km/s.
The heliosphere
The solar wind inflates a vast bubble, the heliosphere, that protects the Solar System from much galactic radiation. Voyager 1 crossed its edge, the heliopause, in 2012 at about 121 AU.
Earth's shield
Earth's magnetic field deflects most of the solar wind, forming the magnetosphere, which is squashed on the Sun side and stretched into a long tail on the night side.

steps: Some particles funnel to the poles

x: The Sun loses about 1.5 million tonnes per second to the solar wind
Comet ion tails point straight away from the Sun because the wind pushes them

deep.x: Mars, without a global magnetic field, had much of its atmosphere stripped by the solar wind.

cards.title: Auroras
cards.text: When solar particles hit the upper atmosphere near the poles, oxygen glows green and red, and nitrogen glows blue and purple: the northern and southern lights.

deep.x: Charged particles from the solar wind and CMEs are funnelled along Earth's magnetic field lines towards the poles. At 100–300 km altitude they collide with oxygen and nitrogen, exciting them to glow, like a neon sign.
Colours and heights
The auroral ovals

Auroras normally form in rings around the magnetic poles: northern Norway, Iceland, Canada and Alaska. During strong storms the ovals expand towards the equator. In May 2024 and October 2024, auroras were photographed from Portugal.

v.unit: Kp index needed to see auroras (approx.)

deep.x: Tips

x: Phone cameras often capture colour the eye can't see in faint auroras
Watch the Kp index and space weather forecasts
Look north, away from city lights

deep.x: Jupiter and Saturn have permanent auroras far more powerful than Earth's, powered partly by their own moons.

cards.title: The Carrington Event
cards.text: In 1859 a huge solar storm made auroras visible near the tropics and gave telegraph operators electric shocks. A similar storm today could damage power grids.

deep.x: On 1 September 1859, British astronomer Richard Carrington saw a brilliant white flare on the Sun. Seventeen hours later, a massive CME hit Earth. Auroras lit up skies as far south as Cuba and Hawaii; people in the Rocky Mountains woke thinking it was dawn.
Telegraph chaos
Telegraph lines sparked and some operators got shocks. Remarkably, some operators disconnected their batteries and sent messages using only the current induced by the storm.
If it happened today

A storm of that size could induce currents that damage high-voltage transformers, causing long blackouts, and could disable many satellites and disrupt GPS. Studies estimate global costs in the trillions.
Near misses

x: 1989: a smaller storm blacked out Quebec for 9 hours
2012: a Carrington-class CME missed Earth by about nine days of orbit

deep.x: Grid operators now have procedures to protect transformers when big storms are forecast.

cards.title: Space weather forecasts
cards.text: Spacecraft watch the Sun to warn of storms a day or more ahead, so satellite and grid operators can prepare.

deep.x: Space weather forecasters watch the Sun constantly, much like meteorologists watch the atmosphere. Spacecraft such as SOHO and the Solar Dynamics Observatory image eruptions, and probes at the L1 point, 1.5 million km sunward, measure the solar wind before it hits Earth.
Scales
Who uses it

x: Power grid operators reduce load on vulnerable transformers
Airlines reroute polar flights to avoid radiation and radio blackouts
Satellite operators safe-mode their spacecraft
Astronauts shelter in shielded parts of the station

deep.x: Forecast limits
It's easy to see a CME leave, but hard to predict how strong its effect will be: that depends on the direction of its magnetic field, only measured when it reaches L1, under an hour before arrival.
Space weather is now listed among national risks in many countries, alongside pandemics and floods.

cards.title: Never look directly
cards.text: Looking at the Sun, even briefly during a partial eclipse, can permanently damage your retina. Use certified eclipse glasses or project the image.

deep.x: The eye's lens focuses sunlight onto the retina like a magnifying glass. Staring at the Sun can burn retinal cells (solar retinopathy) without any pain, because the retina has no pain receptors. Damage can be permanent.
Partial eclipses are the danger
On a normal day, the Sun's glare makes you look away. During a partial eclipse, the sky darkens and people stare longer, but the visible sliver is just as intense.

deep.w: Sunglasses are enough
deep.r: Even dark sunglasses let through far too much light

deep.x: Safe ways

x: Certified eclipse glasses meeting ISO 12312-2
Pinhole projector: a hole in card projecting the Sun onto paper
Telescopes only with proper solar filters on the front
Welding glass of shade 12–14

deep.x: Totality exception
During the brief total phase of a total eclipse, it's safe to look without glasses, but put them back on the moment the Sun reappears.
A colander or the gaps between tree leaves make dozens of tiny crescent images on the ground during a partial eclipse.

cards.title: Parker Solar Probe
cards.text: Launched in 2018, NASA's Parker Solar Probe has flown through the corona and is the fastest human-made object, reaching about 690,000 km/h.

deep.x: Parker Solar Probe, named after Eugene Parker who predicted the solar wind in 1958, is designed to "touch the Sun". On 24 December 2024 it passed just 6.1 million km from the surface, the closest any spacecraft has come.
Surviving the heat

A 11.4 cm thick carbon-composite heat shield faces the Sun at up to about 1,400 °C, while the instruments behind it stay near room temperature. The probe must keep the shield perfectly angled, doing so autonomously.
Getting close is hard

It's harder to reach the Sun than to leave the Solar System: Earth's orbital speed carries you sideways, and you must cancel it to fall in. Parker used seven Venus flybys to slow down and tighten its orbit.
What it's found

x: Magnetic "switchbacks": S-shaped kinks in the solar wind
A dust-free zone near the Sun
Direct measurements inside the corona for the first time

deep.x: Eugene Parker became the first person to see a spacecraft named after him launched, at age 91.

lessons.title: The Big Bang
lessons.summary: How the universe began and grew.

cards.title: An expanding universe
cards.text: In 1929 Edwin Hubble showed that distant galaxies are moving away from us, and the farther they are, the faster. Space itself is expanding.

deep.x: In the 1910s Vesto Slipher measured the spectra of "spiral nebulae" and found most were redshifted: moving away from us. In 1929 Edwin Hubble combined these speeds with distances and found a simple pattern: the farther a galaxy, the faster it recedes.
What it means
This isn't galaxies flying through space away from us in particular. Space itself is stretching, carrying galaxies apart. Every observer in every galaxy would see the same pattern.
Not everything expands
Galaxies, solar systems and atoms don't grow: gravity and other forces hold them together. Expansion only wins over huge distances between galaxy groups.
Einstein originally added a "cosmological constant" to keep the universe static; after Hubble's discovery he dropped it.

cards.title: Run it backwards
cards.text: If everything is moving apart, it was once closer together. Run the film back about 13.8 billion years and everything was extremely hot and dense: the Big Bang.

deep.x: If galaxies are moving apart now, they were closer in the past. Run the expansion backwards and everything converges into a hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago. That early hot phase, and the expansion from it, is what scientists call the Big Bang.

steps: 13.8 billion years ago: the Big Bang

deep.x: Measuring the age
What it doesn't say

The Big Bang theory describes how the universe evolved from a hot, dense state. It doesn't explain what, if anything, came "before" or what caused it; physics as we know it breaks down at the very beginning.

deep.w: The Big Bang explains the origin of everything
deep.r: It describes the evolution from a hot, dense early state; the very beginning is still unknown

deep.x: Three pillars of evidence

x: Galaxies receding in proportion to distance
The cosmic microwave background, leftover heat from the early universe
The amounts of hydrogen, helium and lithium, matching predictions

deep.x: No other theory explains all three pieces of evidence as well.

cards.title: Not an explosion in space
cards.text: The Big Bang wasn't a bomb going off in empty space. It was the rapid expansion of space itself, everywhere at once.

deep.x: The name suggests a bomb going off at a point, with debris flying into empty space. But the Big Bang happened everywhere at once: it was space itself expanding, not things flying through pre-existing space.
No centre
Because every point in space was part of the early dense universe, there's no special place where it "happened". Wherever you are, the Big Bang happened there too.
Faster than light?
Very distant galaxies recede faster than light. That doesn't break relativity: nothing is moving through space faster than light; space between us is stretching.

steps: Distant galaxies recede faster than light

deep.x: Inflation

Many cosmologists think a tiny fraction of a second after the start, space expanded extremely fast, by a factor of at least 10²⁶, in "cosmic inflation". It would explain why the universe is so smooth and flat.
The term "Big Bang" was coined by Fred Hoyle, who didn't believe in it, and the theory's main early proponent was a Catholic priest, Georges Lemaître.

cards.title: Raisin bread
cards.text: Imagine raisins in rising dough: every raisin sees all the others moving away, and the farthest move fastest. There's no centre.

deep.x: Picture a loaf of raisin bread rising in the oven. Each raisin sees every other raisin moving away, and raisins twice as far apart separate twice as fast. No raisin is at the centre.
The balloon version

Another analogy: dots drawn on a balloon spread apart as it inflates. It shows there's no centre on the surface, but suggests a 3D centre inside the balloon, which doesn't exist for the real universe.
Doing the maths
If every distance doubles in an hour, a raisin 1 cm away ends up 2 cm away (moved 1 cm), while one 3 cm away ends up 6 cm away (moved 3 cm). Speed is proportional to distance: exactly Hubble's law.
All analogies break somewhere; the universe may have no edge and may be infinite.

cards.title: The first minutes
cards.text: Within the first three minutes, the universe cooled enough for protons and neutrons to form hydrogen and helium nuclei. Heavier elements came much later, from stars.

deep.x: In the first second, the universe was a hot soup of particles. As it expanded and cooled, quarks bound into protons and neutrons. Between about 1 and 3 minutes, protons and neutrons fused into nuclei: Big Bang nucleosynthesis.
The recipe

By the time fusion stopped, ordinary matter was about 75% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass, with traces of deuterium and lithium. Measurements of the oldest gas clouds and stars match these predictions closely.
Why fusion stopped

The universe was cooling and thinning too fast. Unlike stars, which fuse for billions of years, the early universe had only minutes, so it couldn't build heavy elements. Those came much later, in stars.

steps: Too thin and cold to continue

deep.x: The amount of helium in the universe was a key test: the Big Bang predicted about 25%, and that's what we observe.

cards.title: The afterglow
cards.text: About 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe became transparent. That light still fills space as faint microwaves, found by accident in 1965.

deep.x: For 380,000 years the universe was a glowing fog of charged particles that scattered light. When it cooled to about 3,000 °C, electrons joined nuclei to form neutral atoms and light could travel freely. That light still fills the universe, stretched by expansion into microwaves at 2.7 K (−270 °C).
Found by accident

In 1965 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, testing a radio antenna in New Jersey, found an annoying hiss coming from every direction. They even cleaned pigeon droppings from the antenna. The hiss was the cosmic microwave background (CMB), and they won the 1978 Nobel Prize.
The baby picture of the universe
The CMB is almost perfectly uniform, but has tiny temperature ripples, about 1 part in 100,000. These were the seeds of all later structure: galaxies and clusters grew from them.
About 1% of the static on an old analogue TV tuned between channels came from the cosmic microwave background.

cards.title: Redshift
cards.text: Light from receding galaxies is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths, like a siren dropping in pitch as it drives away.

deep.x: Light from receding objects has its wavelengths stretched towards the red end of the spectrum. For distant galaxies, the stretching is mostly due to space expanding while the light travels: cosmological redshift.
Measuring it

Astronomers find known spectral lines, like hydrogen's, and see how much they've shifted. The redshift "z" says how much the universe has expanded since the light left: z = 1 means wavelengths doubled.
Doppler on Earth
The same principle, for sound, makes an ambulance siren drop in pitch as it passes. Police radar guns use a Doppler shift to measure car speeds.
The record-holding galaxies seen by Webb have redshifts above 14: their light has been stretched more than 15 times.

cards.title: The observable universe
cards.text: We can only see as far as light has had time to reach us. Because space expanded meanwhile, the edge of what we see is about 46 billion light-years away.

deep.x: We can only see objects whose light has had time to reach us since the universe became transparent. Because space kept expanding while the light travelled, the most distant objects we see are now about 46 billion light-years away, not 13.8.
Observable vs entire
The whole universe is likely much larger than the observable part, possibly infinite. What lies beyond our horizon is, in principle, unobservable.
A shrinking view

Because expansion is accelerating, distant galaxies are slipping beyond our reach. In the far future, observers in the Milky Way (merged with Andromeda) would see only their own merged galaxy, with the rest of the universe invisible.

deep.w: The universe is 13.8 billion light-years across
deep.r: The observable part is about 93 billion light-years across, thanks to expansion

deep.x: Being "13.8 billion years old" and "46 billion light-years in radius" aren't contradictory: space stretched while the light travelled.

cards.title: Who named it?
cards.text: Fred Hoyle, who preferred a "steady state" universe, coined "Big Bang" on BBC radio in 1949. Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist, first proposed the idea.

deep.x: In 1927 Georges Lemaître, a Belgian Catholic priest and physicist, proposed that the universe was expanding. In 1931 he suggested it began from a "primeval atom". The idea was controversial for decades.

events.l: Gamow and Alpher's hot Big Bang

deep.x: Steady state
Fred Hoyle, Hermann Bondi and Thomas Gold proposed the steady-state theory: the universe expands, but new matter appears continuously so it always looks the same, with no beginning.
The name

On BBC radio in 1949, Hoyle called the rival theory "this big bang idea". He insisted he didn't mean it as an insult, but the catchy name stuck. The 1965 discovery of the CMB decisively favoured the Big Bang.
Science and faith
Pope Pius XII welcomed the Big Bang as support for creation; Lemaître himself asked him not to mix science and theology so directly, keeping the two separate.
Hoyle, though wrong about steady state, made major contributions, including explaining how stars make carbon.

cards.title: How will it end?
cards.text: Most evidence points to a universe expanding forever, getting colder and darker over unimaginable time: the "heat death". Other endings are still debated.

deep.x: The universe's future depends on dark energy. If it stays constant, as current data mostly suggest, expansion accelerates forever.

items: Big Rip: dark energy tears everything apart
Big Bounce: crunch leads to a new bang

deep.x: The heat death timeline
Why "heat death"?
The universe would reach maximum entropy: everything at the same cold temperature, so no energy flows and nothing can happen. Not hot, but uniform.
New uncertainty
In 2024–25 the DESI galaxy survey reported hints that dark energy may be weakening. If so, the long-term future could change, possibly even towards a slowdown. More data is needed.
These timescales are so vast that the entire history of the universe so far is a tiny flicker at the very start.

quiz.q: How old is the universe?
quiz.explain: Measured from the expansion and afterglow.

quiz.q: What did Hubble discover in 1929?
options: Galaxies are moving away from us

lessons.title: Black holes
lessons.summary: The strangest objects in the universe.

cards.title: The event horizon

items: Event horizon: point of no return

cards.text: A black hole's boundary is the event horizon: the point of no return. Inside, the escape speed exceeds the speed of light.

deep.x: The event horizon is a boundary in spacetime, not a physical surface. Outside it, a rocket with enough thrust can escape. Inside it, every possible path, even for light, leads inward.
Its size
The radius of the event horizon, the Schwarzschild radius, is proportional to mass: about 3 km per solar mass.
What you'd see

x: Approaching, the sky would distort as light bends around the black hole
Behind you, the universe's light would crowd into a shrinking circle
Crossing a large black hole's horizon, you'd notice nothing special at that moment

items.b: ~38 billion km wide, bigger than the Solar System's planets' orbits

deep.w: The event horizon is a solid surface
deep.r: It's an invisible boundary; nothing special happens to a falling observer at that point

deep.x: Once inside, the singularity is not a place in front of you but a moment in your future.

cards.title: How they form
cards.text: Most stellar black holes form when a star more than about 20 times the Sun's mass runs out of fuel and its core collapses.

deep.x: Stellar black holes form when the core of a massive star collapses. Above about 2–3 solar masses, no known force can stop a dead core collapsing: not even the pressure of tightly packed neutrons.
Other routes

items: Direct collapse of gas clouds, early universe
Primordial: maybe from the Big Bang

deep.x: Failed supernovae
Some massive stars may collapse straight into black holes without a bright explosion, simply vanishing. Astronomers have watched a few candidate stars disappear.
Growing
Black holes grow by swallowing gas, stars and other black holes. Mergers detected by gravitational waves often produce black holes of 30–150 solar masses.
The first confirmed black hole, Cygnus X-1, was identified in the 1970s from X-rays emitted by gas falling in from a companion star.

cards.title: Size
cards.text: If the Sun became a black hole, its event horizon would be only about 6 km across. Earth's would be the size of a marble.

deep.x: A black hole's event horizon is surprisingly small for its mass. Squeeze any mass into a small enough sphere and it becomes a black hole.
Density isn't extreme for giants
The average density inside the horizon falls as mass grows. A supermassive black hole of a billion Suns has an average "density" inside its horizon lower than water.

items: average density can be below water's

deep.x: Mass, spin, charge
Physicists say "black holes have no hair": a black hole is fully described by just three numbers: mass, spin and electric charge. All other details of what fell in are hidden.
Spinning black holes drag spacetime around with them, so close in, nothing can stay still relative to distant stars.

cards.title: Supermassive black holes
cards.text: Almost every big galaxy has a supermassive black hole at its centre. Ours, Sagittarius A*, is about 4 million times the Sun's mass.

deep.x: Nearly every large galaxy hosts a central black hole of millions to billions of solar masses. Their masses correlate with their galaxies' bulges, suggesting they grow together.
Quasars

When a supermassive black hole swallows gas rapidly, the surrounding disc heats up and outshines its entire galaxy, sometimes thousands of times over. These are quasars, the brightest steady objects in the universe.
Jets
Magnetic fields near spinning black holes launch jets of particles at nearly light speed, extending hundreds of thousands of light-years. M87's jet is visible in ordinary telescopes.
A puzzle
Webb has found supermassive black holes already existing less than a billion years after the Big Bang. How they grew so big so fast is an active question.
Our own Sgr A* is quiet, eating very little, which is lucky for life in the galaxy.

cards.title: Spaghettification
cards.text: Near a small black hole, gravity pulls far harder on your feet than your head, stretching you like spaghetti.

deep.x: Gravity's pull weakens with distance, so near a black hole the pull on your feet can be much stronger than on your head. This difference, a tidal force, stretches you lengthwise and squeezes you sideways.
Size matters, oddly

Tidal forces at the horizon are strongest for small black holes. Near a stellar black hole, you'd be torn apart long before reaching the horizon. A supermassive black hole's horizon is so big that you could cross it intact and only be spaghettified later.
Tidal disruption events
When a star wanders too close to a supermassive black hole, it's shredded. About half its gas falls in and flares brightly for months. Telescopes catch dozens of these events.
Earth's tides are the same effect, much gentler: the Moon pulls the near side of the oceans more than the far side.

cards.title: Time slows down
cards.text: Near a black hole, time runs slower compared with far away. To a distant observer, something falling in seems to freeze at the edge.

deep.x: General relativity says time passes more slowly in stronger gravity. Near a black hole, the effect becomes extreme. A distant observer watching someone fall in sees their clock slow down and their image redden and fade as they approach the horizon, never quite seeming to cross.

items: sees the faller freeze and fade

deep.x: Interstellar's water planet
In the film *Interstellar*, physicist Kip Thorne helped calculate a planet near a giant spinning black hole where 1 hour equals 7 years on Earth. It's an extreme but physically inspired scenario.

v.unit: time passing elsewhere per hour on the planet

deep.x: Real measurements
Near Sgr A*, astronomers tracked the star S2 passing close in 2018 and measured its light being stretched by gravity, exactly as relativity predicts.
Even Earth's gravity slows time measurably: GPS clocks would drift without correcting for it.

cards.title: Seeing the invisible
cards.text: Black holes are found by their effects: stars orbiting something invisible, glowing hot gas swirling around them and ripples in spacetime.

deep.x: Black holes emit no light, but their surroundings do. Astronomers find them through the effects of their gravity on matter and light around them.
Stars around Sgr A*

For decades, teams led by Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez tracked stars orbiting an invisible point at the Milky Way's centre. The star S2 orbits every 16 years, at up to 2.5% of light speed. Their work won the 2020 Nobel Prize.
X-ray binaries
When a black hole orbits a normal star, it can pull gas off it. The gas heats to millions of degrees as it spirals in, glowing in X-rays.
Lone black holes
In 2022 astronomers detected an isolated black hole wandering through the galaxy by the way it briefly magnified a background star: microlensing.

steps: Black hole passes in front of a star

deep.x: The Milky Way may contain around 100 million stellar black holes, most of them invisible.

cards.title: Gravitational waves
cards.text: In 2015 the LIGO detectors caught ripples in spacetime from two black holes merging 1.3 billion light-years away, as Einstein had predicted a century earlier.

deep.x: Accelerating masses create ripples in spacetime that travel at light speed, stretching and squeezing space as they pass. Einstein predicted them in 1916 but doubted they'd ever be detected: the effect is incredibly small.

steps: Stretch detectors by a fraction of a proton

deep.x: LIGO

Each LIGO detector has two 4 km arms at right angles. Lasers measure the arm lengths; a passing wave changes them by less than 1/10,000 of a proton's width. On 14 September 2015 both LIGO sites detected GW150914: two black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses merging 1.3 billion light-years away.

items.l: solar masses turned into wave energy

deep.x: A new kind of astronomy

Since then, hundreds of mergers have been detected by LIGO, Virgo in Italy and KAGRA in Japan. In 2017 a neutron star merger was seen both in gravitational waves and in light, confirming that such collisions make gold.

events.l: indirect evidence from a binary pulsar
Nobel Prize and neutron star merger

deep.x: Turned into sound
The signal's frequency rises as the black holes spiral in, producing a "chirp" when converted to audio.
The 2015 merger briefly released more power in gravitational waves than all the stars in the observable universe combined emitted as light.

cards.title: The first image
cards.text: In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope, linking radio dishes across the world into an Earth-sized telescope, imaged the shadow of M87's black hole. Sagittarius A* followed in 2022.

deep.x: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) linked radio observatories in Hawaii, Arizona, Mexico, Chile, Spain, the South Pole and elsewhere. Observing together at a 1.3 mm wavelength, they formed a virtual dish the size of Earth, sharp enough to read a newspaper in New York from Paris.

Released on 10 April 2019, the image showed a bright ring of hot gas around a dark shadow: the black hole at the centre of galaxy M87. The ring's size matched Einstein's predictions for a 6.5-billion-Sun black hole.
Sgr A* in 2022

Our own black hole, though much closer, was harder to image because gas around it changes in minutes. The 2022 image showed a similar ring, confirming the physics scales from millions to billions of Suns.
The data was too large to send over the internet: about 5 petabytes, so hard drives were physically shipped.

cards.title: Hawking radiation
cards.text: Stephen Hawking calculated in 1974 that black holes should slowly leak energy and eventually evaporate, though for real ones this takes far longer than the universe's age.

deep.x: In 1974 Stephen Hawking combined quantum theory with general relativity and found that black holes aren't completely black: they should emit faint radiation and slowly lose mass. The smaller the black hole, the hotter it is and the faster it evaporates.
How faint?

A black hole the mass of the Sun would have a temperature of about 60 billionths of a degree above absolute zero, far colder than the cosmic microwave background, so for now it absorbs more than it emits.

items.a: Age of the universe so far

deep.x: The information paradox

If a black hole evaporates into random radiation, what happens to the information about what fell in? Quantum theory says information can't be destroyed. This puzzle remains one of the deepest in physics.
Never observed
Hawking radiation from real black holes is far too faint to detect. Physicists have seen analogous effects in lab systems with sound waves in fluids, called "dumb holes".
Hawking's gravestone in Westminster Abbey is engraved with his formula for black hole temperature.

quiz.q: What is the event horizon?
quiz.explain: Not even light escapes from inside.
