lessons.title: Telescopes and light
lessons.summary: How we see the invisible universe.

cards.title: Looking back in time
cards.text: Light takes time to travel, so we see the Moon as it was 1.3 seconds ago, the Sun 8 minutes ago and Andromeda 2.5 million years ago.

deep.x: Light travels at 300,000 km/s: fast, but not infinitely fast. Everything we see is a message from the past, delayed by the distance it travelled. The farther we look, the older the light.
A time machine for astronomers

Because distant light is old, telescopes can watch the universe's history directly. Webb sees galaxies as they were less than 400 million years after the Big Bang, when the universe was about 3% of its current age.

steps: Distant galaxies: billions of years ago
Cosmic microwave background: 380,000 years after the Big Bang

deep.x: Is that star still there?

For most stars you see, the light left them decades to centuries ago. Stars live millions to billions of years, so almost all are still there; but for a few distant massive stars, we might be seeing a star that has already exploded.

deep.w: Many stars we see are already dead
deep.r: Most naked-eye stars are within a few hundred light-years and still shining

deep.x: Looking out is looking back: the deepest images are also the oldest photographs ever taken.

cards.title: Galileo's telescope
cards.text: In 1609–10 Galileo pointed a simple telescope at the sky and saw Jupiter's moons, the phases of Venus, sunspots and countless stars in the Milky Way.

deep.x: Galileo didn't invent the telescope; Dutch spectacle makers did in 1608. Hearing about it, he built his own, improving it to about 20× magnification, and was the first to point one systematically at the sky.
What he saw

x: **Mountains and craters on the Moon**: it wasn't a perfect heavenly sphere
**Four moons of Jupiter**: proof that not everything orbits Earth
**Phases of Venus**: only possible if Venus orbits the Sun
**Countless stars in the Milky Way**: the universe was bigger than anyone thought

deep.x: Why it was explosive
The phases of Venus in particular contradicted Ptolemy's Earth-centred model. Galileo's support for Copernicus led to his trial by the Inquisition in 1633 and house arrest for the rest of his life.
Galileo's best telescope had a field of view so narrow he could see only a quarter of the full Moon at once.

cards.title: Refractors and reflectors
cards.text: Refracting telescopes use lenses; reflecting telescopes, invented by Newton, use curved mirrors. All big research telescopes are reflectors, because mirrors can be made huge.

deep.x: A refractor bends light with a big lens at the front; a reflector collects light with a curved mirror at the back. Newton built the first practical reflector in 1668 to avoid the coloured fringes that early lenses produced.
Why lenses hit a limit

A lens can only be supported at its edge, so big ones sag under their own weight, and light must pass through flawless glass. The largest refractor ever, at Yerkes Observatory (1897), has a 1-metre lens. Mirrors can be supported from behind, segmented and made enormous.
Modern tricks

x: **Segmented mirrors**: many hexagons acting as one, as on Keck and Webb
**Adaptive optics**: deformable mirrors that cancel atmospheric blur hundreds of times a second
**Interferometry**: combining several telescopes to sharpen detail

deep.x: For backyard astronomy, a simple reflector (a "Dobsonian") gives the most light-gathering power per euro.

cards.title: Bigger is better
cards.text: A telescope's power to collect light depends on its mirror area. The upcoming Extremely Large Telescope in Chile has a 39 m mirror.

deep.x: A telescope's light-gathering power grows with the area of its mirror, which goes with the diameter squared. Double the diameter and you collect four times as much light, seeing fainter, more distant objects.
Sharper too
Bigger mirrors also resolve finer detail, though on the ground the atmosphere blurs the view unless adaptive optics correct it.
The Extremely Large Telescope

ESO's ELT in Chile's Atacama Desert will have a 39 m mirror made of 798 hexagonal segments, collecting more light than all today's large research telescopes combined. Portugal is an ESO member and contributes to its instruments.
The ELT's dome is about 80 m tall, almost as high as the Torre dos Clérigos in Porto (76 m).

cards.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
cards.text: Visible light is a tiny slice of the spectrum. Different wavelengths reveal different things, from cold dust in radio to exploding stars in X-rays.

deep.x: Light is a wave of electric and magnetic fields. Visible light, wavelengths of about 400–700 nanometres, is a sliver of a much larger spectrum, from radio waves metres long to gamma rays smaller than an atom.
What each reveals

items.b: cold gas, pulsars, black hole jets

deep.x: Energy and wavelength
Shorter wavelengths carry more energy per photon. That's why UV burns skin and X-rays pass through it, while radio waves pass harmlessly through your body all day.
Multi-wavelength astronomy
The same object looks completely different across the spectrum. The Crab Nebula glows in radio, infrared, visible, X-ray and gamma rays, each revealing a different process.
Your eyes evolved for visible light because that's where the Sun is brightest and where Earth's atmosphere is transparent.

cards.title: Infrared
cards.text: Infrared light passes through dust clouds and shows cool objects. James Webb sees in infrared to spot newborn stars and the first galaxies, whose light was stretched by expansion.

deep.x: Infrared is light with wavelengths a bit longer than red, felt as heat. Everything warm glows in infrared, including you. Infrared also slips through dust clouds that block visible light, revealing stars being born inside them.

items: shows cool objects and newborn stars

deep.x: Redshift pushes light into infrared

As the universe expands, light from distant galaxies is stretched. Ultraviolet and visible light emitted 13 billion years ago arrives today as infrared. To see the first galaxies, you need an infrared telescope.

steps: Young galaxy emits UV and visible light

deep.x: Why Webb is so cold

An infrared telescope must be colder than what it observes, or its own heat drowns the signal. Webb sits 1.5 million km away, shielded by a five-layer sunshield, at about −233 °C; one instrument is cooled further to −266 °C.
Herschel discovered infrared in 1800 by putting thermometers beyond the red end of a rainbow from a prism and finding it was warmest there.

cards.title: Why go to space?
cards.text: Earth's atmosphere blurs starlight and blocks X-rays, UV and much infrared. Space telescopes avoid both problems.

deep.x: Earth's atmosphere does three annoying things to astronomers: it shimmers (making stars twinkle and images blurry), it glows faintly, and it blocks whole parts of the spectrum.

items: Absorption: blocks X-rays, UV, much infrared

deep.x: What gets through

Only visible light, some infrared and radio reach the ground well. Ozone blocks UV; water vapour blocks much infrared; X-rays and gamma rays are absorbed high up. That's lucky for life, but bad for astronomy.
Ground strikes back

Space telescopes are expensive and hard to repair. Ground telescopes can be much bigger and upgraded easily, and adaptive optics now remove much of the blur. The best sites are high and dry: Chile's Atacama, Hawaii's Mauna Kea, La Palma in the Canaries.
Modern astronomy needs both: space telescopes for sharpness and invisible wavelengths, ground giants for light-gathering power.

cards.title: Radio telescopes
cards.text: Radio telescopes are giant dishes. Linking dishes across continents creates a virtual telescope as wide as the distance between them.

deep.x: Radio waves from space are incredibly faint: all the radio energy ever collected by radio telescopes is less than the energy of a falling snowflake. Huge dishes are needed to gather enough.
History
Karl Jansky discovered radio waves from the Milky Way's centre in 1932 while studying static for Bell Labs. Radio astronomy then found quasars, pulsars and the cosmic microwave background.
Arrays

By combining dishes far apart, astronomers get the sharpness of one telescope as wide as the distance between them. The Event Horizon Telescope linked dishes across the world into an Earth-sized virtual telescope.

items.b: thousands of antennas, South Africa and Australia

deep.x: Protecting radio quiet
Phones, Wi-Fi and satellites cause interference, so radio telescopes are built in remote "radio quiet zones".
Portugal participates in the Square Kilometre Array, the largest radio telescope project in the world.

cards.title: Spectroscopy
cards.text: Splitting starlight into a rainbow reveals dark lines: fingerprints of the elements in the star. That's how we know what stars are made of without visiting.

deep.x: Pass starlight through a prism or grating and it spreads into a rainbow, a spectrum. Atoms of each element absorb light at exact, unique wavelengths, leaving dark lines like a barcode. Matching barcodes reveals what a star is made of.
Helium was found in the Sun first
In 1868, astronomers saw an unknown yellow line in the Sun's spectrum during an eclipse. They named the element helium, after Helios, the Sun. It wasn't found on Earth until 1895.

events.l: Kirchhoff and Bunsen link lines to elements

deep.x: Much more than ingredients
Philosopher's challenge
In 1835 philosopher Auguste Comte said we would never know the chemical composition of stars. Within 25 years, spectroscopy proved him wrong.
Spectroscopy also finds exoplanets (by the star's wobble) and measures the universe's expansion (by redshift).

cards.title: Dark skies
cards.text: Light pollution hides most stars from city dwellers. Portugal's Dark Sky Alqueva reserve was the world's first "Starlight Tourism Destination", certified in 2011.

deep.x: Artificial light at night scatters in the atmosphere and creates skyglow that hides stars. About 80% of the world's population, and more than 99% of people in Europe and the USA, live under light-polluted skies. Most Europeans can't see the Milky Way from home.
Not just astronomy

x: Birds migrating at night are disoriented, and many die hitting lit buildings
Sea turtle hatchlings head towards lights instead of the sea
Insects die around lamps, contributing to insect decline
Night light can disrupt human sleep and hormones

deep.x: Simple fixes

items: Use only the light you need

deep.x: Dark Sky Alqueva

Around the Alqueva lake in the Alentejo, municipalities controlled lighting to protect the night sky. In 2011 it became the world's first Starlight Tourism Destination, with an observatory and stargazing tours.
On a truly dark night you can see around 4,000 stars at once; in central Lisbon, perhaps a few dozen.

quiz.q: Why do we see Andromeda as it was 2.5 million years ago?
options: Its light took that long to reach us
quiz.explain: Light travels at a finite speed.

quiz.q: How do we know what stars are made of?
Why does Webb see in infrared?
options: Light from early galaxies is stretched to infrared

lessons.title: Gravity and orbits
lessons.summary: Why things fall, and why the Moon doesn't.

cards.title: Newton's gravity
cards.text: Isaac Newton realised the force that makes an apple fall also keeps the Moon in orbit. Every mass attracts every other mass.

deep.x: In 1687 Newton published his law of universal gravitation: every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to both masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The same law explains falling apples, tides and planetary orbits.
Gravity is weak

G is tiny, so gravity between everyday objects is minuscule. Two people standing 1 m apart attract with a force less than a millionth of a newton. Gravity only dominates because planets and stars are enormous and it never cancels out, unlike electric charges.
Weighing the Earth
In 1798 Henry Cavendish measured G with a delicate torsion balance in his shed, which let scientists calculate Earth's mass: about 6 × 10²⁴ kg.
Where Newton falls short
Newton's law is superb for spacecraft navigation, but it couldn't explain a small drift in Mercury's orbit. Einstein's general relativity (1915) did.
The apple story is probably partly true: Newton told friends that a falling apple in his family garden set him thinking about gravity.

cards.title: The inverse square law
cards.text: Double the distance and gravity drops to a quarter. Triple it and it drops to a ninth.

deep.x: Gravity spreads out in all directions, like light from a bulb. At twice the distance, the same influence covers four times the area, so it's four times weaker. Many things follow this rule: light, sound and electric force.
Gravity with height
Because Earth's centre is 6,371 km below your feet, going up a few hundred kilometres changes gravity only a little. At the ISS (400 km), it's still about 89% as strong.
Light works the same way
A star twice as far away appears four times dimmer. Astronomers use this to estimate distances to stars whose true brightness they know.
Inverse-square laws appear whenever something spreads evenly from a point into three-dimensional space.

cards.title: Orbits are falling

steps: Fast enough: falls around the Earth

cards.text: An orbiting spacecraft is constantly falling towards Earth but moving sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it. Newton imagined a cannon on a mountain.

deep.x: In his *Principia*, Newton drew a cannon on a very tall mountain. Each faster shot lands farther away; at the right speed, the ball falls towards Earth but the curved surface drops away just as fast, and it circles forever.

steps: Faster still: elliptical orbit or escape

deep.x: Speed depends on height
Lower orbits need higher speeds and are quicker. The ISS at 400 km circles in 92 minutes; the Moon, 384,000 km away, takes 27 days.
Orbital oddities

x: To catch up with something ahead in orbit, you slow down, drop to a lower, faster orbit, then rise again
Speeding up raises your orbit, which makes you slower overall
A dropped spanner keeps orbiting alongside the astronaut who dropped it

deep.x: In orbit you're not floating above gravity; you're falling continually and always missing the ground.

cards.title: Weightlessness

items.r: Gravity is ~90% as strong, they're in free fall

cards.text: Astronauts on the ISS feel weightless not because there's no gravity, which is about 90% as strong there, but because they're falling together with the station.

deep.x: Weight is the feeling of the floor pushing up on you. In a freely falling lift, the floor would fall with you and you'd float. Astronauts in orbit are in permanent free fall along with their station, so nothing pushes on anything: weightlessness.

deep.w: There's no gravity in space
deep.r: At the ISS, gravity is about 89% as strong as on the ground

deep.x: Feeling it on Earth

x: The stomach "drop" at the top of a roller-coaster hill is a moment of free fall
Parabolic flights (the "vomit comet") give about 20–25 seconds of weightlessness per arc
Drop towers give a few seconds for experiments

deep.x: Microgravity
Scientists say "microgravity" because tiny forces remain: air drag, crew moving, the station's rotation. Flames burn as round blue spheres, and water forms floating balls.
Astronauts feel briefly heavy after landing; some have dropped cups, forgetting objects now fall.

cards.title: Mass and weight
cards.text: Your mass stays the same everywhere; your weight depends on gravity. A 70 kg person would weigh about as much as 12 kg on the Moon.

deep.x: Mass is how much matter you contain, measured in kilograms; it's the same anywhere in the universe. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass, measured in newtons. Bathroom scales show "kilograms", but they really measure force and assume Earth's gravity.
Same you, different worlds

v.unit: weight of a 70 kg person, newtons

deep.x: Mass still matters in space

Even weightless, mass resists acceleration: pushing a heavy object in orbit is hard to start and hard to stop. Astronauts measure their body mass with a spring chair that oscillates; heavier people bounce more slowly.
Gravity varies slightly over Earth: you weigh about 0.5% less at the equator than at the poles, due to Earth's spin and bulge.

cards.title: Kepler's laws
cards.text: Johannes Kepler found that planets move in ellipses, sweep equal areas in equal times and that farther planets take longer to orbit.

deep.x: Using Tycho Brahe's precise observations of Mars, Johannes Kepler found three laws of planetary motion between 1609 and 1619, decades before Newton explained why they work.

items: First law: orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus
Second law: a planet sweeps equal areas in equal times

deep.x: The second law in action

A planet speeds up when close to the Sun and slows when far. Earth moves fastest in early January, at perihelion, about 30.3 km/s, and slowest in early July, about 29.3 km/s. That's partly why northern winter is a few days shorter than summer.
The third law
The square of a planet's year is proportional to the cube of its distance. In units of Earth years and AU, period² = distance³ exactly.

x: Jupiter: 5.2 AU

deep.x: Kepler's third law is used today to weigh stars and black holes from the orbits around them.

cards.title: Escape velocity
cards.text: To escape Earth's gravity completely, you'd need about 11.2 km/s. On the Moon, just 2.4 km/s.

deep.x: Escape velocity is the speed needed to coast away from a body forever without further thrust, ignoring air resistance. It depends on the body's mass and radius, not on the mass of the object escaping.
Around the Solar System
Rockets don't need it all at once

Escape velocity applies to a cannonball fired once. Rockets keep firing their engines as they climb, so they can leave gradually. Still, to leave Earth for good, a spacecraft must eventually gain that much energy.
Escaping the Sun
From Earth's orbit, escaping the Sun requires about 42 km/s, but Earth already moves at 30 km/s, so probes need "only" about 12 km/s extra in the right direction.
A black hole is an object whose escape velocity exceeds the speed of light.

cards.title: Gravity assists
cards.text: Spacecraft swing past planets to steal a bit of their orbital speed, like a ball bouncing off a moving train. Voyager used Jupiter and Saturn this way.

deep.x: A spacecraft flying close behind a moving planet gets pulled along and leaves faster, relative to the Sun. The planet loses an immeasurably tiny bit of orbital speed in exchange. Flying in front of a planet does the opposite and slows the craft down.
The train analogy
Throw a tennis ball at an approaching train: it bounces back faster than you threw it, having picked up the train's speed. The planet is the train; gravity is the bounce.
Famous slingshots

x: Voyager 2 used Jupiter, Saturn and Uranus to reach Neptune in 12 years instead of 30
Parker Solar Probe used Venus seven times to slow down and fall towards the Sun
Rosetta used Earth three times and Mars once to catch a comet

deep.x: Discovered by a student
In 1961 UCLA student Michael Minovitch used computers to calculate gravity-assist trajectories, showing they could make outer-planet missions practical.
Gravity assists are free fuel: they let small spacecraft reach places their rockets alone never could.

cards.title: Lagrange points

items.b: between Sun and Earth, solar observatories

cards.text: There are five points where a small object can hold position relative to two big bodies. Webb sits at L2, 1.5 million km from Earth, opposite the Sun.

deep.x: Around any two orbiting bodies, like the Sun and Earth, there are five points where gravity and orbital motion balance, so a small spacecraft can stay in the same position relative to both. Joseph-Louis Lagrange worked them out in 1772.

items.b: 1.5 million km sunward, SOHO watches the Sun
1.5 million km outward, Webb and Gaia

deep.x: Stable and unstable

L1, L2 and L3 are like balancing on a hilltop: spacecraft need small engine burns every few weeks to stay. L4 and L5 are like valleys: objects naturally collect there. Jupiter has thousands of "Trojan" asteroids at its L4 and L5 points.
Why L2 for Webb
At L2, the Sun, Earth and Moon are all on one side, so a single sunshield blocks them all, keeping the telescope cold. And it stays in constant contact with Earth.
NASA's Lucy mission, launched in 2021, is touring Jupiter's Trojan asteroids, named after heroes of the Trojan War.

cards.title: Geostationary orbit
cards.text: At about 36,000 km up, a satellite orbits once a day, staying over the same spot. TV satellite dishes point at a fixed point in the sky for this reason.

deep.x: At 35,786 km above the equator, an orbit takes exactly one sidereal day. A satellite there moves as fast as Earth turns beneath it, appearing fixed in the sky. Science-fiction author Arthur C. Clarke popularised the idea for communications in 1945.
Uses

x: TV broadcasting: dishes can be fixed in one direction
Weather satellites watching the same half of Earth continuously, like Meteosat for Europe
Some communications and military satellites

deep.x: Downsides
The great distance means a radio delay of about 0.25 s for a round trip: noticeable on phone calls and online games. And geostationary satellites can't see the polar regions well.
A crowded ring
There's only one geostationary ring, so slots are allocated by the International Telecommunication Union. Old satellites are boosted a few hundred km higher into a "graveyard orbit".
In Portugal, satellite TV dishes point roughly south, about 40° up, towards satellites above the equator.

quiz.q: Why are astronauts on the ISS weightless?
options: They're in free fall with the station
quiz.explain: Gravity is still about 90% as strong.

quiz.q: Double the distance, and gravity becomes…

lessons.title: Time, space and Einstein
lessons.summary: Relativity without the maths homework.

cards.title: The speed of light

items.l: laps of Earth in a second

cards.text: Light travels at about 300,000 km per second in a vacuum, and every observer measures the same speed, however fast they move. That simple fact changes everything.

deep.x: In 1887 Michelson and Morley expected the speed of light to vary with Earth's motion through space; it didn't. In 1905, Einstein took this as a principle: light in a vacuum always moves at the same speed, c, for every observer, however fast they're moving.
Why that's strange

If you throw a ball forwards from a moving train, its speed adds to the train's. But shine a torch forwards from a rocket at half light speed, and both you and a watcher on the ground measure the light at exactly c. For that to work, time and space themselves must adjust.
Defining the metre
Since 1983 the speed of light has been fixed by definition, and the metre is defined as the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second.

x: Light takes 1.3 s to reach the Moon and about 0.13 s to circle Earth
In glass or water, light slows, but c in a vacuum is the universal limit

deep.x: c isn't really about light: it's the speed limit of cause and effect in the universe.

cards.title: Time dilation
cards.text: Moving clocks run slow. An astronaut travelling near light speed would return to find more time had passed on Earth than for them.

deep.x: If light's speed is the same for everyone, moving clocks must tick slowly from the point of view of someone watching them pass. The effect is tiny at everyday speeds and huge near light speed.
How big?
Evidence

x: **Muons**: particles made high in the atmosphere live only 2.2 microseconds, too short to reach the ground, yet many do, because their clocks run slow at 99.9% of c
**Atomic clocks on planes** (Hafele–Keating, 1971) showed the predicted tiny differences
**Particle accelerators** see fast unstable particles live longer exactly as predicted

deep.w: Time dilation is just a clock error
deep.r: Every process slows, including ageing; time itself runs differently

deep.x: Astronauts on the ISS age about 0.01 seconds less than us over six months.

cards.title: The twin paradox
cards.text: One twin flies to a star at 87% of light speed and back; the other stays home. On return, the traveller has aged about half as much. Time dilation itself has been confirmed with atomic clocks flown on planes.

deep.x: Twin A stays on Earth; twin B flies to a star 10 light-years away at 87% of c and returns. Earth clocks show about 23 years; B's ship clocks show about 11.5 years. B comes back younger.
Why is it a "paradox"?

From B's view, Earth moved away and back, so shouldn't A be younger? The situations aren't symmetric: B accelerates, turns around and decelerates, switching reference frames. A stays in one frame the whole time. Calculations from either side agree: the traveller ages less.
A one-way ticket to the future
Time dilation makes travel to the future possible in principle: go fast enough and you return to a distant future. Travel to the past is a different matter, with no known way to do it.
Cosmonaut Gennady Padalka, after 879 days in orbit, is about 0.02 seconds younger than if he'd stayed on Earth.

cards.title: Length contraction
cards.text: Objects moving very fast are shorter in their direction of motion, as measured by someone watching them pass. It's only noticeable near light speed.

deep.x: Objects moving fast are measured as shorter along their direction of motion by an observer they're passing. A spaceship flying at 87% of c would appear half as long as it is at rest.
Hand in hand with time dilation

The muon example shows both views: from the ground, the muon's clock runs slow; from the muon's view, the atmosphere is squashed thin, so it reaches the ground in time. Both descriptions agree on the result.
What it doesn't do

x: It doesn't squash objects physically; it's about measurements between frames
The traveller notices nothing odd on their own ship
At everyday speeds it's far too small to measure

deep.x: Very fast objects would actually look rotated rather than squashed in photos, an effect called Terrell rotation, because light from different parts takes different times to reach the camera.

cards.title: E = mc²

items.m: speed of light squared, a huge number

cards.text: Mass and energy are two forms of the same thing. A tiny amount of mass holds huge energy, which powers the Sun and nuclear reactors.

deep.x: Published by Einstein in 1905 as a follow-up to special relativity, E = mc² says mass and energy are equivalent. Because c² is huge (9 × 10¹⁶), a tiny bit of mass is equivalent to a vast amount of energy.

x: 1 gram of mass
= 9 × 10¹³ joules ≈ 25 million kWh

deep.x: Where it shows up

x: **The Sun**: converts about 4 million tonnes of mass to energy each second
**Nuclear power**: splitting uranium releases energy as products weigh slightly less
**Particle physics**: collisions turn energy into new particles of matter

deep.x: A common misunderstanding
E = mc² doesn't mean things easily turn into energy. In fission only about 0.1% of the mass is converted; in fusion about 0.7%. Total conversion happens only when matter meets antimatter.
Even chemistry
When you burn wood, the products weigh very slightly less than the wood and oxygen did, but the difference is far too small to measure.
A paperclip's worth of mass (1 g), fully converted, would supply the electricity of a Portuguese town of about 5,000 people for a year.

cards.title: Gravity bends spacetime
cards.text: In general relativity (1915), mass curves spacetime and objects follow the curves. Think of a heavy ball on a trampoline making marbles roll towards it.

deep.x: In 1915 Einstein's general relativity replaced Newton's force of gravity with geometry: mass and energy curve spacetime, and objects move along the straightest possible paths through that curved spacetime. "Spacetime tells matter how to move; matter tells spacetime how to curve," as John Wheeler put it.
The trampoline picture
A heavy ball on a trampoline makes a dip; marbles roll towards it. It's a helpful image but imperfect: in real spacetime, time itself is curved too, which is what mostly makes things fall.
Predictions confirmed
Gravity slows time
Clocks run slower in stronger gravity. A clock at sea level runs slightly slower than one at the top of a mountain. Modern atomic clocks detect the difference over just 1 cm of height.
Your head ages slightly faster than your feet, about 90 billionths of a second over a lifetime.

cards.title: Light bends
cards.text: In 1919, Arthur Eddington measured starlight bending around the Sun during an eclipse, exactly as Einstein predicted. It made Einstein world famous.

deep.x: If gravity curves spacetime, light passing a massive object should bend. Einstein predicted that starlight grazing the Sun would shift by 1.75 arcseconds, twice what a Newtonian calculation gave.
The 1919 eclipse

Stars near the Sun are normally hidden by its glare, so Arthur Eddington organised expeditions to photograph them during the total eclipse of 29 May 1919: one to Sobral in Brazil and one to Príncipe, then a Portuguese colony off Africa. Their measurements favoured Einstein.
Overnight fame
On 7 November 1919, *The Times* headline read "Revolution in Science". Einstein became a global celebrity almost overnight.

x: The Príncipe expedition is commemorated in São Tomé and Príncipe and in Portuguese science history
Later radio measurements confirmed the bending to better than 0.01%

deep.x: Eddington's team was nearly clouded out on Príncipe; the clouds cleared only partly during totality.

cards.title: GPS needs relativity
cards.text: GPS satellites' clocks run faster by about 38 microseconds a day because of weaker gravity and slower because of speed. Without corrections, positions would drift by kilometres daily.

deep.x: GPS satellites carry atomic clocks and orbit at 20,200 km, moving at about 14,000 km/h. Two relativistic effects change their clocks' rates compared with clocks on the ground.

items.b: speed slows the clocks by ~7 µs a day
weaker gravity speeds them by ~45 µs a day

deep.x: Why microseconds matter

GPS works by timing signals that travel at light speed. A timing error of 1 microsecond means a position error of about 300 m. Uncorrected, 38 µs a day would accumulate into errors of around 10 km a day.
The fix
Engineers set satellite clocks to tick slightly slower before launch, at 10.22999999543 MHz instead of 10.23 MHz, so that in orbit they match ground time.
Every time your phone finds your location, it's quietly confirming Einstein.

cards.title: Gravitational lensing
cards.text: Massive galaxy clusters bend light from galaxies behind them, creating arcs and multiple images. Astronomers use these natural magnifying glasses.

deep.x: Massive objects bend light from things behind them, acting as cosmic lenses. A galaxy cluster can magnify, distort and multiply the image of a distant galaxy into arcs or even a complete ring.

items: Weak: slight distortions, mapping dark matter

deep.x: Einstein rings
When source, lens and observer line up perfectly, the background galaxy appears as a ring around the lens. Webb and Hubble have imaged many.
Uses

x: **Natural telescopes**: lensing magnifies faint early galaxies Webb couldn't otherwise see
**Dark matter maps**: lensing reveals mass we can't see
**Finding exoplanets**: a star passing in front of another briefly brightens it; a planet adds a tell-tale blip

deep.x: A lensed supernova, "Refsdal", appeared four times around a galaxy in 2014, and astronomers correctly predicted a fifth image would appear about a year later.

cards.title: Nothing faster than light
cards.text: Nothing with mass can reach light speed: the closer you get, the more energy each extra bit of speed costs. Information can't travel faster than light either.

deep.x: As an object with mass speeds up, the energy needed to accelerate it further rises without limit as it approaches c. Reaching light speed would take infinite energy, so particles with mass can only get closer and closer.
Fastest so far

x: The LHC accelerates protons to 99.9999991% of c
Parker Solar Probe, the fastest spacecraft, reached about 0.064% of c
Light itself has no mass, so it always travels at c

deep.x: Causality
If information could travel faster than light, some observers would see effects before their causes. Relativity's speed limit protects cause and effect.
Loopholes that aren't

items.b: space stretches, distant galaxies recede faster than c

deep.x: The universe's speed limit means the nearest stars, let alone other galaxies, will remain years to millions of years away, even for light.

quiz.q: What happens to a clock moving very fast?
Why does GPS need relativity?
options: Satellite clocks run at a different rate
quiz.explain: Uncorrected, errors grow by km a day.

lessons.title: Life as an astronaut
lessons.summary: Eating, sleeping and working in orbit.

cards.title: Becoming an astronaut
cards.text: Space agencies pick a handful from thousands of applicants. ESA's 2022 selection drew over 22,500 applications for 17 places, including astronauts and reserves.

deep.x: Agencies look for people who are healthy, calm under pressure, good team players and expert in something useful: medicine, engineering, science or flying. Candidates go through rounds of tests over more than a year.
Typical requirements (ESA)

x: A master's degree in science, engineering, medicine or maths, or test-pilot training
Several years of professional experience
Fluent English; other languages a plus
Height roughly 150–190 cm and good health; glasses are allowed

deep.x: Not just superhumans

Agencies stress teamwork and resilience more than athletic prowess. In 2022 ESA also selected John McFall, a Paralympic sprinter and surgeon, as the first "parastronaut" to study whether people with a physical disability can fly in space.
Portugal joined ESA in 2000, so Portuguese citizens can apply to ESA astronaut selections.

cards.title: Training
cards.text: Astronauts train for years: spacewalks rehearsed underwater, survival training, Russian language, robotics and flights in planes that create short bursts of weightlessness.

deep.x: Basic training takes about a year; mission-specific training can take two more. Astronauts must master the station's systems, science experiments, robotics and emergencies.
Underwater spacewalks

NASA's Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory is a pool 62 m long and 12 m deep holding a full-size ISS mock-up. Weighted suits make astronauts neither float nor sink, imitating weightlessness for six-hour sessions.
The skills list

items: Survival training in forest, sea and caves

deep.x: Expeditionary skills
ESA's CAVES programme sends astronauts underground for days to practise teamwork in isolation. Survival training covers landing off course in the wilderness, a real risk with capsules.
Much training is about failure: fire, depressurisation and toxic leaks are rehearsed until responses become automatic.
Astronauts learn to fly jets and keep flying them; NASA uses T-38 trainers to practise fast decision-making.

cards.title: Eating in space
cards.text: Food comes in pouches and tins; crumbs are dangerous, so tortillas replace bread. Taste dulls in orbit, so astronauts love spicy sauces.

deep.x: Space food has come a long way from 1960s tubes of paste. ISS crews choose from about 200 items: thermostabilised, freeze-dried, irradiated and fresh fruit when cargo arrives.
Rules of the table

x: No crumbs: they float into eyes and equipment, so tortillas replace bread
Salt and pepper come as liquids
Food sticks to forks by surface tension; drinks are sipped from pouches
Fizzy drinks don't work well: gas and liquid don't separate in the stomach

deep.x: Taste changes
Fluid shifting to the head causes a "stuffy nose" feeling, dulling smell and taste. Astronauts often crave hot sauces and strong flavours.
Growing food
Astronauts have grown lettuce, radishes, chillies and flowers in the Veggie chamber. Future Mars missions will need much more home-grown food.
In 1965 astronaut John Young smuggled a corned-beef sandwich onto Gemini 3; its crumbs caused a fuss in Congress.

cards.title: Sleeping

items: Sleeping bag tied to the wall

cards.text: Astronauts sleep in small cabins in sleeping bags tied to the wall. There's no "up", so you can sleep in any orientation.

deep.x: Each ISS astronaut has a small private crew quarter, the size of a phone booth, with a sleeping bag strapped to the wall, a laptop and a light. Without gravity there's no need for a bed: you just float in the bag.

items: Sleeping bag tied to the wall
Eye mask for 16 sunrises a day

deep.x: Why ventilation matters
In weightlessness, warm breath doesn't rise. Exhaled CO₂ can pool around your face, causing headaches, so crew quarters need constant airflow.

steps: No convection to carry CO₂ away

deep.x: Sleep problems

x: Crews average about 6 hours a night, less than on Earth
16 sunrises a day disrupt the body clock, so lighting is tuned to mimic day and night
Some astronauts' arms float up in front of them while asleep

deep.x: Station "night" follows UTC (Greenwich time), so on the ISS everyone lives on London's clock, Portugal's winter time.

cards.title: Bodies in space
cards.text: Without gravity, muscles and bones weaken, fluids shift to the head, and the spine stretches; astronauts grow about 3 cm taller temporarily.

deep.x: Weightlessness affects nearly every body system. Without the constant load of gravity, the body adapts as if those muscles and bones aren't needed.
Puffy face, bird legs
About 2 litres of fluid shift from the legs to the upper body. Astronauts get puffy faces and thin "bird legs" in the first days.
Space adaptation
Over half of astronauts get space sickness during the first two or three days: nausea and disorientation as the brain reinterprets the inner ear's signals.
The Twin Study

In 2015–16 NASA compared astronaut Scott Kelly, who spent nearly a year in orbit, with his identical twin Mark on Earth. Most changes, in genes, immune system and microbes, returned to normal after landing; a few persisted.
Astronauts grow up to about 3 cm taller in orbit as their spine discs expand; they shrink back on return, sometimes with back pain.

cards.title: Exercise

items.l: bone lost a month without it

cards.text: To fight bone and muscle loss, ISS crews exercise about two hours a day on a treadmill with harnesses, a bike and a resistance machine.

deep.x: Exercise is the main defence against bone and muscle loss. ISS crews exercise about 2 hours a day, six days a week, as part of their work schedule.

items.b: running in a harness pulling them down
resistance machine using vacuum cylinders, like lifting weights

deep.x: How the machines work

In weightlessness, free weights weigh nothing. The ARED resistance device uses vacuum cylinders to create up to about 270 kg of resistance for squats and deadlifts. Treadmills use bungee harnesses to pull runners onto the belt.
It works, partly
Modern exercise regimes have greatly reduced muscle loss and helped protect bone, though some bone loss still occurs. Diet with enough vitamin D and calories helps too.
These lessons help on Earth too: research on astronaut bones informs osteoporosis treatment.

cards.title: Water recycling
cards.text: On the ISS, about 98% of water, including sweat and urine, is recycled into clean drinking water.

deep.x: Water is heavy to launch, so the ISS recycles almost everything: urine, sweat, shower water and even moisture from the air. In 2023 its system reached 98% water recovery.
The "coffee" joke
Astronauts joke that "yesterday's coffee becomes today's coffee". The recycled water is cleaner than most tap water on Earth.
Air too

x: Oxygen is made by splitting water with electricity (electrolysis)
CO₂ is scrubbed from the air; some is combined with hydrogen to make more water
Trace gases are filtered to avoid build-up

deep.x: Why it matters for Mars
A Mars trip would last 2–3 years with no resupply. Closed-loop life support that recycles water and air almost completely is essential.
The same technologies have been adapted for water purification in disaster zones and remote villages on Earth.

cards.title: Spacewalks
cards.text: Spacewalks last six to eight hours. The suit is a mini spaceship with oxygen, cooling and pressure. Astronauts stay tethered at all times.

deep.x: A spacewalk, or EVA (extravehicular activity), is one of the riskiest jobs in space. Astronauts install equipment, repair the station and fix science instruments, working in pairs and always tethered.
The suit

A spacesuit is a one-person spacecraft: it provides oxygen, removes CO₂, protects against micrometeoroids and temperature extremes from about −150 °C to +120 °C, and has water-cooled underwear to remove body heat.
Preparing
Suits run at lower pressure than the station, so astronauts first breathe pure oxygen to purge nitrogen from their blood, avoiding the bends, like divers.
Real dangers

x: In 1965 Leonov's suit ballooned; he had to vent air to get back inside
In 2013 Luca Parmitano's helmet filled with water, nearly drowning him
Hands tire quickly working against stiff, pressurised gloves

deep.x: Stiff gloves cause fingernail damage, so astronauts often trim nails very short before spacewalks.

cards.title: The overview effect
cards.text: Many astronauts describe a shift in perspective after seeing Earth from space: a fragile blue ball with no visible borders.

deep.x: Author Frank White coined "the overview effect" in 1987 for the shift in perception many astronauts describe: seeing Earth whole, with no visible borders and a paper-thin atmosphere, creates a sense of unity and fragility.
In their words
Astronauts often say the atmosphere looks like a thin blue line, "like the skin of an apple". Many return with stronger feelings about protecting the planet.
Earth seen from orbit

x: Sunrises and sunsets every 45 minutes
Lightning flashing across storm clouds
Auroras below the station
The Sahara's dust blowing over the Atlantic

deep.x: Researchers study whether virtual reality can give people on Earth a taste of the overview effect.

cards.title: Coming home
cards.text: After months in orbit, astronauts need weeks to readapt: balance is shaky, and things feel heavy. Some forget gravity and let go of objects mid-air.

deep.x: Returning from months in orbit is physically hard. The brain has adapted to weightlessness, so on return gravity feels overwhelming: heads feel heavy, walking is wobbly and turning causes dizziness.
The landing

Soyuz capsules land under parachutes on the steppes of Kazakhstan, firing small rockets a metre above the ground. Crew Dragon splashes down in the ocean. Recovery teams help crews out, often in reclining chairs.
Rehabilitation

x: About 45 days of supervised rehabilitation with physiotherapists
Bone density can take years to recover, and some loss may be permanent
Astronauts report forgetting gravity: letting go of cups, expecting them to float

deep.x: ESA astronaut Tim Peake said that after landing even his tongue felt heavy, making it hard to speak at first.

Why do astronauts get taller in space?

lessons.summary: Finding your way around the night sky.

cards.title: Constellations

items.l: stars visible on a dark night

cards.text: Constellations are patterns of stars named by ancient cultures. Astronomers recognise 88 official ones. Their stars are usually not close to each other in space.

deep.x: A constellation is a pattern of stars, and since 1922 also an official region of the sky. The International Astronomical Union recognises 88 constellations that together tile the entire sky, so every star belongs to exactly one.
Patterns aren't neighbours
Stars in a constellation usually lie at very different distances. The stars of Orion's belt are about 700–1,300 light-years away, unrelated to each other except by line of sight.
Asterisms
Some famous patterns aren't official constellations. The Big Dipper (or Plough) is part of Ursa Major; the Summer Triangle links stars from three constellations.
Many cultures, many skies
Aboriginal Australians saw an "Emu in the Sky" in dark dust lanes; Chinese astronomers divided the sky into 28 lunar mansions; Polynesian navigators used star paths to cross the Pacific.
Several southern constellations, like Telescopium and Microscopium, were named by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in the 1750s after scientific instruments.

cards.title: Finding the North Star
cards.text: Follow the two end stars of the Big Dipper's "bowl" upwards about five times their distance to reach Polaris, which barely moves and marks north.

deep.x: Polaris lies almost exactly above Earth's North Pole, so as Earth spins, it stays nearly fixed while other stars circle around it. Its altitude above the horizon equals your latitude: about 39° in Lisbon.

steps: Two pointer stars on the bowl

deep.x: Not the brightest
Polaris is only about the 48th brightest star: moderately bright, not dazzling. People often expect it to be brighter.

deep.w: The North Star is the brightest star in the sky
deep.r: It's only moderately bright; Sirius is the brightest

deep.x: Navigation
Sailors, including Portuguese navigators, measured Polaris' height with quadrants and astrolabes to find their latitude. Near the equator, Polaris sinks to the horizon; south of it, it's invisible.
Pole stars change
Earth's axis wobbles in a 26,000-year cycle (precession). About 4,500 years ago the pole star was Thuban; in about 12,000 years it will be Vega.
No equivalent bright star marks the South Pole; southern navigators use the Southern Cross instead.

cards.title: The sky turns
cards.text: Stars rise in the east and set in the west because Earth rotates. Long-exposure photos turn stars into circles around the celestial pole.

deep.x: As Earth rotates west to east, the whole sky appears to turn east to west around the celestial poles, once every 23 hours 56 minutes. Stars near Polaris never set; they're called circumpolar.
Circumpolar stars
From Portugal, stars within about 39° of Polaris never set, including the Big Dipper and Cassiopeia. Farther south, fewer stars are circumpolar.
Star trails
A long-exposure photo pointed at Polaris shows stars as concentric arcs. A full circle would need a 24-hour exposure in darkness, only possible in polar winter.
Earlier each night
Each night, a star rises about 4 minutes earlier, adding up to 2 hours a month. That's why the constellations shift with the seasons.
The 4-minute difference is why a sidereal day (23 h 56 min) is shorter than a solar day.

cards.title: Seasonal stars
cards.text: As Earth orbits the Sun, we see different constellations at night through the year. Orion rules winter evenings; Scorpius summer ones.

deep.x: At night we look away from the Sun. As Earth orbits, the night side faces different directions in space, so different constellations dominate the evening sky through the year.
The zodiac

The Sun appears to move through 13 constellations along the ecliptic over a year, including Ophiuchus, which astrology ignores. The traditional zodiac dates are also off by about a month because of precession.

items.b: 12 signs, fixed dates from ~2,000 years ago
13 constellations on the ecliptic, dates shifted

deep.x: Highlights from Portugal

x: **Winter**: Orion, Sirius, the Pleiades cluster
**Spring**: Leo's sickle, Arcturus
**Summer**: the Milky Way through Sagittarius and Scorpius, low in the south
**Autumn**: the Andromeda galaxy, Pegasus' great square

deep.w: Your zodiac sign is the constellation the Sun was in at your birth
deep.r: Due to precession, the Sun was usually in the previous constellation

cards.title: Orion
cards.text: Orion is easy to find: three bright stars in a row form his belt. Red Betelgeuse marks a shoulder and blue Rigel a foot.

deep.x: Orion, the Hunter, is one of the most recognisable constellations, visible from almost anywhere on Earth because it straddles the celestial equator. It dominates winter evenings in the Northern Hemisphere.
The Orion Nebula

Below the belt, Orion's "sword" contains a fuzzy patch: the Orion Nebula, a stellar nursery 1,300 light-years away where thousands of stars are forming. It's visible with the naked eye on dark nights and stunning in binoculars.
Betelgeuse

Betelgeuse is a red supergiant so large that, placed where the Sun is, it would extend past the orbit of Mars, maybe Jupiter. In 2019–20 it dimmed dramatically after belching out a dust cloud: the "Great Dimming".
A signpost

x: Follow the belt downwards to Sirius, the brightest star
Follow it upwards to Aldebaran and the Pleiades

deep.x: Orion's belt points almost exactly towards Sirius, so the belt is a pointer to the night sky's brightest star.

cards.title: Star brightness
cards.text: Astronomers measure brightness in magnitudes: lower numbers are brighter. Sirius, the brightest night star, is −1.5; the faintest naked-eye stars are about +6.

deep.x: Ancient astronomer Hipparchus ranked stars from 1st magnitude (brightest) to 6th (faintest visible). The modern scale keeps that backwards system and makes it precise: each step of 1 magnitude means about 2.5 times brighter; 5 magnitudes means exactly 100 times.
The scale
Apparent vs absolute

Apparent magnitude is how bright a star looks from Earth; absolute magnitude is how bright it would look from a standard distance of 32.6 light-years. Sirius looks bright mainly because it's close; Rigel looks fainter but is far more luminous.
Hubble can detect objects around magnitude 31, about 10 billion times fainter than the faintest star you can see.

cards.title: Planets wander

steps: A month later: moved against the stars

cards.text: "Planet" comes from the Greek for "wanderer": planets move against the background stars over weeks, staying close to the Sun's path, the ecliptic.

deep.x: Ancient sky-watchers noticed five bright "stars" that moved against the fixed constellations: the planets, from the Greek *planētēs*, "wanderer". All stay close to the ecliptic, because the Solar System is flat.

steps: Weeks later: moved along the ecliptic

deep.x: Retrograde motion
Sometimes a planet seems to stop and move backwards for weeks. This happens when Earth, on its faster inside track, overtakes an outer planet, like passing a slower car on a motorway.
Mercury retrograde
Mercury appears to go retrograde about three times a year. Astronomically it's just a viewing angle; it has no effect on phones, emails or relationships.

deep.w: Mercury retrograde causes chaos
deep.r: It's an optical effect of orbital motion with no influence on Earth

deep.x: Conjunctions

When planets appear close together in the sky, it's a conjunction: a lovely sight, though they're actually hundreds of millions of km apart. In December 2020, Jupiter and Saturn appeared closer than at any time since 1623.
Copernicus' explanation of retrograde motion was one of the strongest arguments for a Sun-centred Solar System.

cards.title: The Milky Way band
cards.text: On a dark night, a pale band arches across the sky: the combined light of billions of stars in our galaxy's disc, seen edge-on from inside.

deep.x: The Milky Way is shaped like a thin disc. From inside, looking along the disc we see a band crowded with stars; looking out of it, we see far fewer. The band's dark lanes are clouds of dust blocking distant starlight.

steps: We sit inside a flat disc
Look along it: band of stars

deep.x: Best seen

x: On moonless nights away from cities, ideally where the sky is rated Bortle 1–3
From Portugal, the brightest part, towards the galactic centre in Sagittarius, is low in the south in summer
The Alentejo and the interior mountains have some of Europe's darkest skies

deep.x: Its name

The Greeks saw spilled milk from the goddess Hera: *galaxias*, from *gala*, milk, gave us "galaxy". In Portuguese it's the Via Láctea, and pilgrims once called it the Way of St James, guiding to Santiago de Compostela.
Galileo was the first to show with a telescope, in 1610, that the Milky Way's glow is made of countless faint stars.

cards.title: Using your eyes

items: Look slightly to the side of faint objects

cards.text: Your eyes need 20–30 minutes in darkness to fully adapt. Use a red light to read maps, because red barely disturbs night vision.

deep.x: Your eye adapts to darkness in two stages: pupils widen within seconds, then the retina's rod cells build up a light-sensitive pigment, rhodopsin, over 20–30 minutes. One glance at a bright phone resets much of it.
Tricks of experienced observers

x: **Red light**: rods are almost blind to deep red, so red torches preserve night vision
**Averted vision**: look slightly to the side of a faint object; the edges of the retina have more rods
**Breathing and comfort**: a reclining chair and warm clothes help you stay patient
**Phone apps** with night mode turn the screen red

deep.x: Why stars look colourless
Faint light is seen by rods, which don't sense colour, so most stars look white. Bright stars like Betelgeuse and Rigel show their orange and blue tints.
Use binoculars before a telescope: 7×50 or 10×50 binoculars show craters, moons of Jupiter and star clusters.

cards.title: A first night out
cards.text: Pick a moonless night, go away from lights, start with the Moon or a bright planet, then find Orion or the Big Dipper. Binoculars show far more than you'd expect.

deep.x: Good stargazing needs a plan. Check the Moon phase (new Moon is best for faint objects), the weather and cloud forecasts, and a dark location.

items: Bring warm clothes and a red light

deep.x: A beginner's route
What to try with binoculars

x: The Moon's craters, best along the shadow line, not at full Moon
Jupiter's four big moons
The Pleiades star cluster
The Andromeda galaxy, a faint smudge 2.5 million light-years away

deep.x: Events to plan for

x: Meteor showers: Perseids in August, Geminids in December
Eclipses and planetary conjunctions
ISS passes, listed on apps and websites

deep.x: In Portugal, astronomy clubs and Ciência Viva centres hold free public observing nights with telescopes.

lessons.title: Asteroids, comets and impacts
lessons.summary: Space rocks and how we defend Earth.

cards.title: The asteroid belt

items.w: A crowded field of tumbling rocks
items.r: Mostly empty space, probes fly through safely

cards.text: Between Mars and Jupiter orbit millions of rocky bodies. Despite films, they're spread out: spacecraft cross the belt without dodging anything.

deep.x: The main belt lies between Mars and Jupiter, about 2.1 to 3.3 AU from the Sun. It contains more than a million asteroids over 1 km, yet its total mass is only about 3% of the Moon's, and half of that is in four bodies: Ceres, Vesta, Pallas and Hygiea.
Why no planet formed
Jupiter's strong gravity stirred up the region, making collisions too violent for rocks to stick together. Many fragments were flung out, leaving a sparse belt.
Mostly empty space
The average distance between asteroids over 1 km is around a million km. More than a dozen spacecraft have crossed the belt without needing to dodge.

deep.w: The belt is a dense field of rocks
deep.r: Typical gaps are hundreds of thousands to millions of km

deep.x: Families
Collisions shatter larger asteroids into "families" sharing similar orbits. Vesta's family came from a giant impact that also sent meteorites to Earth; we have pieces of Vesta in museums.
Kirkwood gaps, empty zones in the belt, mark orbits where Jupiter's regular tugs clear asteroids out.

cards.title: Ceres
cards.text: Ceres, the largest object in the asteroid belt at about 940 km wide, is classed as a dwarf planet. NASA's Dawn found bright salt deposits on its surface.

deep.x: Ceres, discovered by Giuseppe Piazzi on 1 January 1801, was first called a planet, then an asteroid, and since 2006 a dwarf planet. It's the only dwarf planet in the inner Solar System and is large enough to be round.
Dawn's discoveries

NASA's Dawn spacecraft, using efficient ion engines, orbited first Vesta and then Ceres. It found bright spots in Occator Crater: deposits of sodium carbonate salts left by briny water seeping up from below.
A wet world

x: Ceres may be about a quarter water ice by mass
It has ammonia-bearing clays, suggesting it formed farther out and migrated inwards
Organic molecules were detected on its surface

deep.x: Dawn was the first spacecraft to orbit two different bodies beyond the Earth–Moon system.

cards.title: Comet anatomy

items: Tails: point away from the Sun
Nucleus: icy core, a few km

cards.text: A comet is a "dirty snowball" of ice and dust a few km wide. Near the Sun, ice turns to gas, forming a glowing head and tails that always point away from the Sun.

deep.x: A comet's nucleus is a dark, porous lump of ice, dust and organic material, typically 1–20 km across, darker than charcoal. Far from the Sun it's inert. Within roughly 3 AU, sunlight turns ice directly into gas, which drags dust with it.

items: Ion tail: blue, straight, pushed by solar wind

deep.x: Two tails

The **ion tail** is made of charged gas swept straight back by the solar wind, glowing blue. The **dust tail** is pushed more gently by sunlight pressure and curves along the comet's path. Both point away from the Sun, even when the comet moves outwards.
Rosetta

ESA's Rosetta orbited comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko for two years (2014–16) and dropped the Philae lander on it. The comet was shaped like a rubber duck and smelled, according to its gas, of rotten eggs, ammonia and almonds.

events.l: Rosetta lands on the comet, mission ends

deep.x: Comet tails can stretch over 100 million km, nearly the Earth–Sun distance.

cards.title: Halley's Comet
cards.text: Edmond Halley predicted in 1705 that a comet seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 would return in 1758. It did, after his death. It next returns in 2061.

deep.x: Halley's Comet returns roughly every 76 years. Edmond Halley, using Newton's new laws, realised that comets seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 were the same object and predicted its return in late 1758. It reappeared on Christmas night 1758, after Halley's death, a triumph for Newtonian physics.
Halley in history

x: Its 1066 appearance was seen as an omen before the Battle of Hastings and embroidered on the Bayeux Tapestry
Giotto painted it as the Star of Bethlehem around 1305
In 1910 Earth passed through its tail, and some sold "comet pills" to frightened people

deep.x: The 1986 flotilla
Spacecraft from Europe, the USSR and Japan met the comet. ESA's Giotto flew within 600 km of the nucleus and photographed it: a dark, peanut-shaped body 15 km long with jets of gas.
Meteor showers from Halley
Dust shed by Halley produces two meteor showers each year: the Eta Aquariids in May and the Orionids in October.
Mark Twain was born in 1835 during Halley's appearance and predicted he'd die when it returned; he died in 1910, the day after its perihelion.

cards.title: Where comets come from
cards.text: Short-period comets come from the Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune; long-period ones from the distant Oort Cloud, a shell perhaps a light-year away.

deep.x: Comets are frozen leftovers from the outer Solar System. They're stored in two great reservoirs and occasionally nudged inwards.
The Oort Cloud

Proposed by Jan Oort in 1950, the Oort Cloud may contain trillions of icy bodies, extending perhaps a light-year or more. It has never been seen directly; its existence is inferred from comets arriving from all directions with very long orbits.
How comets get nudged
Interstellar visitors
Some comets come from other stars entirely. 'Oumuamua (2017), 2I/Borisov (2019) and 3I/ATLAS (2025) passed through our Solar System on one-time paths, carrying material from other planetary systems.
Long-period comets can appear with little warning; Hale–Bopp in 1997 was visible to the naked eye for 18 months.

cards.title: The dinosaur killer
cards.text: About 66 million years ago, an asteroid around 10 km wide hit Mexico's Yucatán, making the Chicxulub crater. Dust and fires changed the climate and ended the non-bird dinosaurs.

deep.x: About 66 million years ago, an asteroid about 10 km wide struck what is now the Yucatán Peninsula at around 20 km/s. The Chicxulub crater it left is about 180 km wide, now buried under sediment.
The evidence

In 1980 Luis and Walter Alvarez found a thin clay layer worldwide, rich in iridium, an element rare on Earth's surface but common in asteroids, exactly at the boundary between the Cretaceous and the Paleogene. The crater itself was identified in 1991.
Winners and losers

x: All non-bird dinosaurs, pterosaurs and most marine reptiles disappeared
Small mammals, birds, crocodiles and turtles survived
Mammals then diversified, eventually including us

deep.x: Volcanoes too?
India's Deccan Traps erupted vast lava floods around the same time, adding climate stress. Most scientists now see the impact as the main trigger.
The asteroid hit sulphur-rich rock; if it had struck deep ocean, the climate effects and extinction might have been much smaller.

cards.title: Tunguska
cards.text: In 1908 an object exploded over Siberia, flattening about 80 million trees over 2,000 km². Nobody was killed because the area was so remote.

deep.x: On 30 June 1908, a fireball exploded over the Podkamennaya Tunguska River in Siberia, about 5–10 km above the ground. It was probably a stony asteroid or comet fragment roughly 50–60 m wide.
No crater
Because it exploded in the air, there was no crater. Trees at the centre were stripped but left standing, while those further out were flattened radially, pointing away from the blast.
Late investigation
The remote area wasn't studied until Leonid Kulik's expedition in 1927. Eyewitnesses 60 km away described being thrown from their chairs and feeling intense heat.
If it hit a city
An air burst of that size over a big city would cause enormous destruction. That's part of why 30 June is now Asteroid Day, to raise awareness of impact risks.
For several nights after the event, skies over Europe were so bright that people could read newspapers outdoors at midnight.

cards.title: Chelyabinsk
cards.text: In 2013 a 20-metre rock exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia. The shock wave shattered windows and injured about 1,500 people, mostly from flying glass.

deep.x: On 15 February 2013, a 20 m, 12,000-tonne asteroid entered over Russia at about 19 km/s. It exploded about 30 km up with the energy of roughly 500 kilotons of TNT, about 30 Hiroshima bombs.
Why people were hurt
The flash was brighter than the Sun. Curious residents went to windows to look, and about a minute later the shock wave arrived, shattering glass. Most injuries came from flying glass.
Unseen until it hit
It came from the direction of the Sun, where telescopes can't look, so nobody saw it coming. By coincidence, a different, unrelated asteroid passed close to Earth the same day.
Lessons

x: Even small asteroids can cause damage
Dashcams in Russia captured the event, giving scientists precise trajectories
It boosted funding for telescopes to find smaller asteroids

deep.x: A 650 kg fragment was recovered from Lake Chebarkul and is displayed in a local museum.

cards.title: Planetary defence
cards.text: Telescopes track near-Earth asteroids. In 2022 NASA's DART spacecraft crashed into the moonlet Dimorphos and changed its orbit: the first test of deflecting an asteroid.

deep.x: Planetary defence is about finding dangerous asteroids early and, if necessary, changing their path. Survey telescopes have found over 95% of near-Earth asteroids larger than 1 km; the hunt continues for smaller ones.
DART

On 26 September 2022 NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, a 160 m moonlet orbiting the asteroid Didymos, at 6.1 km/s. It shortened Dimorphos' orbit by 33 minutes, far more than the minimum goal of 73 seconds, partly because ejected debris acted like a rocket.
Hera
ESA's Hera mission, launched in 2024, will reach Didymos in 2026 to study the crater and measure Dimorphos' mass, turning DART into a repeatable technique.
Other options

x: Kinetic impactor: hit it hard, like DART
Gravity tractor: hover nearby for years, gently pulling it off course
Nuclear device: last resort for large, late-detected threats

deep.x: The key is time: a tiny nudge decades in advance is far easier than a big push weeks before impact.

cards.title: How worried should we be?
cards.text: Small rocks hit every day and burn up. Bigger impacts are rare: city-destroying ones about every few centuries, and dinosaur-killers every ~100 million years.

deep.x: Impact risk is low probability but high consequence. The smaller the object, the more often it arrives, and the less harm it does.

items.b: every couple of weeks, burns up

deep.x: Known threats

No known asteroid has a significant chance of hitting Earth in the next century. Apophis, 340 m, will pass safely at about 32,000 km on 13 April 2029, closer than geostationary satellites and visible to the naked eye from Europe.
The Torino scale

Astronomers rate impact threats from 0 (no hazard) to 10 (certain global catastrophe). Almost all objects sit at 0. When an asteroid briefly scores higher, extra observations nearly always bring it back to 0.
In perspective
Your lifetime risk of dying in an impact is extremely small but not zero, comparable to some rare natural hazards. Unlike earthquakes, though, impacts are preventable with enough warning.
NASA's NEO Surveyor telescope, planned for launch around 2027, is designed to find most near-Earth asteroids larger than 140 m.

lessons.title: Dark matter and dark energy
lessons.summary: The 95% of the universe we can't see.

cards.title: What the universe is made of
cards.text: Ordinary matter, everything made of atoms, is only about 5% of the universe. The rest is dark matter and dark energy, which we can't see directly.

deep.x: Measurements of the cosmic microwave background, galaxy clusters and supernovae all agree on the universe's recipe: about 5% ordinary matter, 27% dark matter and 68% dark energy.
Even ordinary matter is mostly hidden
Of the 5% that's ordinary matter, only a small part is in stars. Most is hot, thin gas between galaxies, hard to detect.
How we know

x: The pattern of hot and cold spots in the cosmic microwave background depends on these amounts
Galaxy rotation and cluster motions show extra unseen mass
Distant supernovae reveal accelerating expansion

deep.x: Everything humans have ever seen through any telescope makes up about 5% of what's out there.

cards.title: Spinning too fast
cards.text: In the 1970s Vera Rubin found that stars at galaxy edges orbit as fast as those near the centre. Visible matter alone couldn't hold them; something unseen adds gravity.

deep.x: In a solar system, outer planets move slower than inner ones because most mass is at the centre. Astronomers expected the same for stars in galaxies. In the 1970s Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured galaxy rotation and found outer stars moving just as fast as inner ones: "flat rotation curves".
The interpretation
Flat rotation curves mean galaxies must contain much more mass than we see, spread in a large halo extending far beyond the visible disc. Without it, the outer stars would fly off.

items: Dark matter halo: most of the mass

deep.x: Vera Rubin's legacy

Rubin faced barriers as a woman in astronomy, yet her work became the cornerstone evidence for dark matter. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which released its first images in 2025, bears her name.
In the Milky Way, dark matter may outweigh stars and gas by about 5 to 1, perhaps more including the full halo.

cards.title: Fritz Zwicky
cards.text: Back in 1933, Fritz Zwicky noticed galaxies in the Coma Cluster moved too fast to be held together by visible matter. He called the missing mass "dunkle Materie", dark matter.

deep.x: Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky, working at Caltech, studied the Coma Cluster in 1933. Galaxies were moving so fast that the cluster should have flown apart, unless it contained hundreds of times more mass than its visible light suggested. He called it "dunkle Materie".

steps: Far more than the visible stars

deep.x: Ignored for decades
His conclusion was largely overlooked for 40 years, partly because his estimates were rough and partly because he was famously abrasive. Rubin's rotation curves in the 1970s brought the idea back.
A prolific mind
Zwicky also coined "supernova" with Walter Baade and proposed that supernovae create neutron stars, years before neutron stars were found.
Good ideas can wait decades for evidence and attention to catch up.

cards.title: The Bullet Cluster
cards.text: When two galaxy clusters collided, the hot gas slowed down, but most of the mass, mapped by lensing, passed straight through: strong evidence for dark matter.

deep.x: The Bullet Cluster is two galaxy clusters that collided about 150 million years ago, 3.7 billion light-years away. It offered one of the most direct pieces of evidence that dark matter is a real substance, not just a quirk of gravity.

steps: Gas clouds smash and slow down
Galaxies and dark matter pass through
Mass and gas end up separated

deep.x: Two maps compared
X-ray telescopes (Chandra) mapped the hot gas, which holds most of the ordinary matter. Gravitational lensing mapped where the mass actually is. The mass sat with the galaxies, not with the gas.
Why it matters
Alternative theories that modify gravity struggle to explain mass located away from most ordinary matter. Dark matter that barely interacts, passing through like ghosts, explains it naturally.
The "bullet" is a shock wave of hot gas shaped like a bullet, moving at about 4,500 km/s.

cards.title: What could it be?
cards.text: Dark matter doesn't emit or absorb light and barely interacts. Candidates include unknown particles like WIMPs or axions. Detectors deep underground have found nothing so far.

deep.x: Dark matter must have mass and gravity but almost no interaction with light or ordinary matter. It can't be ordinary atoms, which would show up in measurements of the early universe, so physicists look for new particles.
How we hunt

x: **Direct detection**: huge tanks of liquid xenon deep underground wait for a dark matter particle to bump a nucleus
**Indirect detection**: telescopes look for radiation from dark matter particles annihilating
**Colliders**: the LHC tries to create dark matter particles

deep.x: Modified gravity
A minority of physicists propose that gravity behaves differently at very low accelerations (MOND). It explains galaxy rotation well but struggles with clusters and the cosmic microwave background.
Billions of dark matter particles may be passing through your body every second without leaving any trace.

cards.title: Dark energy
cards.text: In 1998 two teams found that the universe's expansion is speeding up, not slowing. Something, called dark energy, pushes space apart. It won the 2011 Nobel Prize.

deep.x: In 1998 two teams measuring distant Type Ia supernovae found they were fainter, so farther, than expected. The universe's expansion is accelerating. Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess won the 2011 Nobel Prize.
What might it be?
The simplest explanation is Einstein's "cosmological constant": an energy belonging to empty space itself. As space expands, there's more of it, so its push grows relative to matter's pull.
A cosmic tug-of-war
For the first ~9 billion years, gravity slowed the expansion. About 5 billion years ago, dark energy took over and expansion started to accelerate.
Is it changing?
Recent results from the DESI survey (2024–25) hint that dark energy might be weakening over time. If confirmed, it would change our picture of the universe's future.
Einstein called his cosmological constant his "biggest blunder"; it may turn out to be one of his best ideas.

cards.title: Standard candles
cards.text: Type Ia supernovae all peak at about the same brightness, so how bright they look tells us how far away they are, like judging distance by a known light bulb.

deep.x: To measure distance, astronomers need objects whose true brightness they know: "standard candles". Comparing true and apparent brightness gives distance, just as you can judge how far away a 100 W bulb is from how dim it looks.
The cosmic distance ladder

items: Type Ia supernovae: billions of ly

deep.x: Type Ia supernovae

They happen when a white dwarf in a binary system gains matter until it reaches about 1.4 Suns and explodes. Because they explode at a similar mass, their peak brightness is similar, and so bright they're visible across billions of light-years.
The Hubble tension
Measuring the expansion rate with the distance ladder gives about 73 km/s per megaparsec; measuring it from the early universe gives about 67. This "Hubble tension" may signal new physics.
Henrietta Leavitt's 1912 discovery of the Cepheid period–luminosity rule made the first rungs of the ladder possible.

cards.title: The cosmic web
cards.text: On the largest scales, galaxies form a web of filaments and walls around huge empty voids, shaped by dark matter's gravity.

deep.x: Maps of millions of galaxies reveal a vast web: galaxies gather along filaments and sheets, with clusters at the knots, surrounding enormous voids up to hundreds of millions of light-years across.
How it formed

Tiny density ripples in the early universe, visible in the cosmic microwave background, grew under gravity. Dark matter collapsed first into a scaffolding; ordinary gas flowed along it and formed galaxies at the densest points.

steps: Tiny ripples after the Big Bang

deep.x: Simulations
Supercomputer simulations like Millennium and IllustrisTNG start from early-universe conditions, add dark matter and physics, and reproduce a web that looks strikingly like the real one.
Our place
The Milky Way sits in a modest filament near the edge of the Local Void. Galaxy surveys have mapped the Laniakea Supercluster, our "immeasurable heaven", about 500 million light-years across.
The cosmic web's structure looks remarkably similar to networks of neurons in the brain, though the similarity is only visual.

cards.title: Euclid
cards.text: ESA's Euclid telescope, launched in 2023, is mapping billions of galaxies to measure how dark matter and dark energy shaped the universe.

deep.x: ESA's Euclid space telescope, launched on 1 July 2023, sits at the L2 point and is mapping a third of the sky. Its goal: a 3D map of billions of galaxies over 10 billion years of cosmic history to understand dark matter and dark energy.
Two techniques

x: **Weak lensing**: measures tiny distortions in galaxy shapes, revealing the dark matter between us and them
**Galaxy clustering**: measures how galaxies are spaced at different eras, tracking expansion

deep.x: A wide view
Euclid's field of view is about 2.5 times the area of the full Moon, much wider than Hubble or Webb, letting it survey huge areas efficiently.
Portuguese astronomers contribute to the Euclid Consortium, including science teams at the Institute of Astrophysics and Space Sciences in Lisbon and Porto.

cards.title: Science at the edge
cards.text: Dark matter and dark energy are names for things we can measure but don't yet understand. Not knowing is where the most exciting science happens.

deep.x: Dark matter and dark energy are placeholders: names for effects we can measure precisely without knowing their cause. That's normal in science. Neptune began as "something pulling Uranus"; Mercury's odd orbit led to relativity.
Possible futures
The open questions

x: What is dark matter made of?
Is dark energy constant, or does it evolve?
Why is the Hubble constant measured differently by different methods?
Are these signs of a deeper theory linking gravity and quantum physics?

deep.x: Admitting what we don't know is the start of discovery; the 95% we don't understand is where the next revolutions may come from.

quiz.q: What fraction of the universe is ordinary matter?
quiz.explain: The rest is dark matter and dark energy.
